candidates.title: A THREE-STAGE GENERALIZED SCALING LAW FOR LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL PRE-TRAINING
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire their capabilities primarily through scaling, and the rapidly rising cost of training has turned compute-budget allocation into a central practical concern. Classical scaling laws express loss as a function of model size and data volume only, and therefore cannot quantify data quality or domain mixture, two factors that are increasingly decisive in modern pre-training. This paper develops a three-stage framework for a generalized scaling law. First, the classical power law is fitted to 1,176 standardized Pythia training points by multi-start nonlinear least squares, with row- and block-bootstrap confidence intervals. Second, four quality-augmented candidate forms are compared on a held-out N-D-Q experiment grid; the additive form, in which the quality penalty enters linearly with the quality deficit, is selected, and a large supplementary matrix is identified as contaminated by its reversed quality monotonicity, its violations of the entropy floor, and the sign reversal of its quality coefficient when pooled. Third, the law is unified with centered-log-ratio domain-mixture coordinates, from which equal-loss substitution rates, elasticities, and compute-normalized marginal gains are derived analytically. The classical law attains an RMSE of 0.00011 nat with stable exponents across five data sources; the quality law reaches a hold-out correlation of 0.99; and the predictions remain accurate for models up to ten trillion parameters, where quality improvement proves up to 30,000 times more cost-effective than parameter scaling. The framework thus provides a quantitative basis for compute-constrained resource allocation in LLM pre-training.

candidates.title: Lightweight constraint aware retrieval augmented question answering for machining process planning
candidates.abstract: Machining process planning requires technical answers that respect locating datums, operation sequences, machining allowances, and process capability. This study presents Lite-CRAG, a lightweight constraint-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) method for Chinese machining questions. It targets a persistent weakness of RAG outputs in manufacturing: fluent answers that omit required engineering content or violate domain constraints. The method combines character-bigram TF-IDF retrieval with intent-triggered checklists and deterministic verification followed by up to three local revision rounds, and revision requires no additional language-model call. A knowledge base of 303 entries grouped into 37 documents supported evaluation on 53 questions across five machining categories. All methods used Gemma 3 4B for generation and Qwen3 4B for automated reference-answer assessment; answer accuracy denotes acceptance under an automated reference-coverage rubric rather than expert judgement. Lite-CRAG achieved 83.0% answer accuracy and a 13.2% rule-detected violation rate, compared with 71.7% and 50.9% for Naive-RAG, which used the same retriever. Ablation showed that bounded local revision accounted for the larger effect: removing it reduced accuracy to 71.7% and increased the violation rate to 43.4%, whereas removing checklist injection yielded 81.1% and 18.9%. These findings indicate that explicit checklists and inexpensive deterministic output revision can improve reference coverage and internal rule consistency of RAG outputs for machining process planning at low computational cost, offering an inspectable, trustworthy-AI-oriented alternative to additional model calls.

candidates.title: Evaluating transformer based language model robustness under low rate training data poisoning
candidates.abstract: Abstract Purpose The recent adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in educational technologies, such as writing assistants, question answering systems, educational assessments, and tutoring raises concerns about the models’ trustworthiness and the potential that knowledge generated by these systems may be compromised. The present work explores whether transformer-based models are susceptible to training-data poisoning and whether a small fraction of poisoned training data can impact classification performance on a downstream legal text classification task. Methodology Label flipping and semantic perturbation were evaluated using controlled experiments on the ECHR-A multi-label legal text classification task from the LexGLUE benchmark. Three transformer-based model architectures (BERT, T5, DistilGPT) were considered at poisoning rates of 0.5%, 1%, 2%, and 5%. Performance was evaluated on a clean test set using element-wise accuracy and exact-match accuracy, with macro-precision, macro-recall, and macro-F1 reported where available. These different metrics reflect the need to not only evaluate label prediction correctness but also complete prediction correctness for multi-label tasks. Findings Initial experiments suggest that a small amount of poisoned training data may impact the performance of transformer-based models on downstream tasks. However, the evidence remains limited: controlled repeated-seed BERT comparisons did not show statistically significant differences after Bonferroni correction, and not all experimental conditions across the three architectures were repeated across multiple seeds. The comparison of element-wise and exact-match accuracy also highlights the importance of considering complementary metrics when interpreting model performance and potential poisoning effects in multi-label classification. Novelty The present work provides preliminary empirical observations of low-rate training-data poisoning across different transformer-based architectures and highlights methodological considerations for evaluating training-data poisoned models.

candidates.title: Conversational AI Agents in Physical Rehabilitation: A Scoping Review with Implications for Physiotherapy Practice in Greece
candidates.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI), ranging from rule-based chatbots to agents built on large language models (LLMs), is increasingly being applied in physical rehabilitation, yet little synthesized evidence exists on how these systems are used clinically and what their adoption would require within specific national health systems such as that of Greece. This scoping review, conducted according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, mapped the architectures, interaction modalities, clinical use cases, and reported the effectiveness of conversational AI in physical rehabilitation and considered the relevance of these findings for Greek physiotherapy practice. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, arXiv, and Google Scholar were searched for studies published between 2010 and 2026 that evaluated conversational AI in physical therapy or musculoskeletal care. Nine primary empirical studies were included, while national policy documents and health regulations were reviewed separately to assess feasibility in the Greek context. The included studies examined embodied virtual coaches, mobile text chatbots, LLM-based advisors, and robot-integrated conversational systems, which were used mainly for exercise coaching, postoperative follow-up, adherence monitoring, and patient reassurance. Feasibility, user satisfaction, and short-term engagement were consistently high, but rigorous long-term trials of clinical efficacy were scarce. In Greece, deployment would require adaptation to the Greek language, professional governance, and alignment with EOPYY reimbursement structures and the EU AI Act. Conversational AI therefore appears to be a promising adjunct to physical rehabilitation, whose responsible adoption should proceed in phases with linguistic localization and clear regulatory safeguards. candidates.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE LEARNING AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF SPEECH SKILLS
candidates.abstract: This article analyzes current opportunities for using artificial intelligence in foreign language learning and in the development of learners’ speech skills. The relevance of the study is determined by the rapid development of digital technologies and the spread of generative artificial intelligence, large language models, chatbots, and automatic speech recognition systems, which are gradually becoming integrated into the educational process. The aim of the article is to provide a theoretical rationale for the pedagogical potential of artificial intelligence in foreign language education and to identify opportunities for its use in developing speaking, listening, reading, writing, lexical, and grammatical competences. The methodological basis of the study includes analysis, systematization, comparison, and generalization of the results of recent scholarly works, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and empirical studies devoted to the use of artificial intelligence technologies in foreign language learning. Particular attention is paid to generative chatbots as a means of creating an additional communicative environment, modeling professional situations, personalizing learning, and providing immediate feedback. The article analyzes the potential of artificial intelligence for developing productive and receptive speech skills, as well as its possible impact on learners’ motivation, willingness to communicate in a foreign language, and speaking anxiety. The main advantages of using AI in foreign language training are identified, including individualization of the educational process, increased opportunities for language practice, accessibility of learning, immediate feedback, and the ability to model diverse communicative situations. At the same time, the risks associated with unreliable AI-generated content, academic integrity, data privacy, digital inequality, and the possibility of learners becoming overly dependent on technology are considered. The article substantiates the position that artificial intelligence should be viewed not as a replacement for the teacher, but as a pedagogical support tool that, when used methodically and appropriately, can complement traditional and interactive forms of foreign language instruction. The pedagogical conditions for effective integration of artificial intelligence into the development of foreign-language communicative competence are identified.

candidates.title: Knowledge compression and knowledge graph-based retrieval-augmented generation for large language models in dairy cow precision feeding
candidates.abstract: Abstract Knowledge for dairy cow precision feeding is dispersed across nutritional standards, scientific literature and professional resources, complicating evidence-supported question answering with large language models (LLMs). We integrated a curated domain corpus with LightRAG, an existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework combining knowledge graphs and vector retrieval. Corpus preparation comprised PDF-to-Markdown conversion, two-stage rule-based cleaning and document-level knowledge compression. Compression prioritised feeding-relevant evidence, numerical values, units and applicability conditions while retaining source identifiers, reducing cleaned literature text by 95.53%. The final corpus contained 2,925 documents and 6,992,080 non-whitespace characters, yielding 5,610 text chunks, 52,509 entities and 64,863 relations. We evaluated DeepSeek v4, Qwen 3.7 Max and GLM 5.3 with and without LightRAG on 100 frozen questions, obtaining 600 responses independently scored by ChatGPT and Kimi-k3 using the same blinded rubric. ChatGPT mean question–answer matching scores increased from 55.8 to 78.7, 43.5 to 79.2 and 65.3 to 80.2, respectively; Kimi-k3 scores increased from 39.8 to 80.6, 31.6 to 80.3 and 44.7 to 82.8. LightRAG-enhanced responses scored higher in 299 of 300 ChatGPT comparisons and 298 of 300 Kimi-k3 comparisons. These findings support curated knowledge and hybrid retrieval to improve question–answer matching for dairy cow precision feeding under the specified evaluation protocol.

candidates.title: SAMSeeK: nervous centralis lesion diagnostic report generation via SAM 2 and vision-language models
candidates.abstract: Objective This study investigates the capability of visual language models (VLMs) in generating accurate diagnostic reports for neurological disorders of the central nervous system. To address the critical challenge of background-induced misclassification, we propose a novel framework that enables joint lesion segmentation, quantitative analysis, and report generation—thereby improving the reliability and clinical relevance of automated brain lesion diagnosis. Methods We present SAMSeeK , a unified model that integrates a geometry-aware vision encoder with a large VLM. To overcome the limitations of conventional sequential modeling in capturing spatially heterogeneous brain lesions, we incorporate Hilbert curve-guided scanning into the Mamba architecture and redesign both the encoder and decoder of SAM 2 to enhance local-global contextual awareness of lesion regions. Furthermore, we introduce a structured prompt enhancement mechanism that injects quantitative lesion attributes—such as volume, spatial coordinates, and pixel-level extent—into Qwen 2.5-VL to ground report generation in anatomically precise information. The model is trained and evaluated on a curated dataset of 4,800 2D brain MRI slices spanning three major pathologies: glioma, epilepsy (including focal cortical dysplasia), and cerebral infarction, and validated across three public benchmarks (BraTS2021, FCD2023, ISLES2022). Results SAMSeeK achieves state-of-the-art performance in both segmentation and classification. It attains an average Dice coefficient of 82.4% and IoU of 73.5% on BraTS2021, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. In lesion-type classification, it reaches 81.2% accuracy , 83.6% precision , 83.9% recall , and an F1-score of 0.852 . Leveraging these capabilities, SAMSeeK successfully generated 4,800 clinically plausible diagnostic reports, each enriched with quantitative lesion descriptors. Conclusion By synergizing Hilbert-enhanced spatial modeling with VLM-driven semantic reasoning, SAMSeeK effectively mitigates background interference and significantly improves lesion localization and classification accuracy. The framework demonstrates strong potential as a reliable tool for automated, interpretable, and quantitative brain lesion report generation in clinical neuroimaging workflows.

candidates.title: Performance of Reasoning-intensive Large Language Models on the Orthopaedic In-training Examination
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Reasoning-intensive large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in orthopaedic education, but their reliability remains uncertain. We compared two next-generation reasoning models, ChatGPT 5.2 Extended Thinking (ET) and Claude Opus 4.5 ET, on the Orthopaedic In-training Examination (OITE), emphasizing multimodal interpretation and reasoning quality. METHODS: Using a zero-shot prompting protocol, each model was administered 622 OITE questions (280 image-based, 342 text-only) from the 2022 to 2024 examinations archived on AAOS ResStudy, with every question entered into a new, temporary chat session to prevent memory carryover. Because both models answered identical questions, between-model accuracy was compared using the McNemar test, with risk differences expressed as 95% Newcombe confidence intervals; within-model image versus text performance was compared using the chi-square test. For 2024 (n = 202), responses were additionally graded by two-rater consensus as ideal or nonideal based on answer correctness and reasoning quality. RESULTS: ChatGPT achieved 88.1% (548/622) overall accuracy versus 81.7% (508/622) for Claude (P < 0.001). The advantage was most pronounced on image-based questions (84.6% vs 75.4%; risk difference 9.3 percentage points, 95% CI 4.7 to 14.0; P < 0.001) and smaller on text-only items (90.9% vs 86.8%; P = 0.040). Both models exceeded the PGY-5 resident mean (70 to 73%) and the ABOS Part I minimal passing standard (62.5 to 68.6%). ChatGPT produced more ideal responses on 2024 questions (87.1% vs 76.7%) and more explanations consistent with the AAOS rationale (87.6% vs 78.2%), with Claude showing a greater quality decrement on image-based questions. DISCUSSION: Reasoning-intensive LLMs scored above published PGY-5 resident means on archived OITE items, with ChatGPT 5.2 ET outperforming Claude Opus 4.5 ET, particularly on multimodal items. Because residents completed the full examination and the models a smaller archived subset, resident comparisons are descriptive only. Persistent image-based errors and confidently incorrect reasoning support an adjunctive, rather than authoritative, educational role.

candidates.title: Evaluating Tool-Assisted Multimodal Large Language Models: A Benchmarking Methodology with Applications to Image Quality Assessment and Enhancement
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can interpret visual inputs and invoke external tools, but these capabilities do not necessarily translate into reliable or effective data processing. Evaluating their use of user-defined tools requires examining both the quality of the resulting outputs and the behavior of the execution process. We propose a benchmarking methodology and configurable framework for assessing MLLMs operating with pre-registered diagnostic and data manipulation tools. We demonstrate the methodology through image-quality assessment and enhancement using three open MLLMs and images affected by blur, contrast, noise, and brightness degradations. The evaluation combines agreement with human quality scores, reference-based enhancement metrics, controlled tool and reference-access configurations, and comparisons with fixed-parameter baselines and reference-informed parameter sweeps. The results show that stronger quality assessment does not consistently translate into better enhancement and that outcomes depend on the model, available tools, and evaluation metric. On matched test images, fixed-parameter denoising achieves larger SSIM and LPIPS improvements than the evaluated agents, while execution reliability also differs substantially across model configurations. These findings demonstrate how the framework can expose limitations and trade-offs in tool-mediated image processing, supporting systematic evaluation of MLLMs within explicitly defined tool environments.

candidates.title: Designing a Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Cultural Interpretation at Kotta Cinna
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in digital cultural heritage has focused largely on reconstruction and visualisation, while systems that help visitors interpret a site through dialogue remain scarce, and generative models risk producing fluent but unsupported historical claims. This paper reports the needs analysis, design, and implementation phases of a Design-Based Research study that develops an AI-driven cultural interpretation system for Kotta Cinna, an 11th–14th century archaeological site in Medan, Indonesia, where visitor engagement is low and on-site interpretation is limited. Design requirements derived from documented site problems were mapped onto four design dimensions—narrative quality, transparency, interactivity, and adaptivity—and realised as a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline: BGE-M3 multilingual dense retrieval over a curated, expert-verified knowledge base, a relevance gate that declines out-of-scope questions, and the SEA-LION language model, which composes narratives with citations to their source passages. Visitors reach the system through QR codes at five site zones that also supply location context. Black-box functional testing with deterministic stand-in models confirmed eleven required behaviours, including cited answers, refusal of out-of-scope questions, multi-turn follow-up questions, and correct computation of evaluation metrics; several early design defects were detected and corrected through this testing. A technical evaluation protocol based on a 100-query benchmark is specified to measure retrieval precision and recall, refusal accuracy, expert-rated faithfulness with inter-rater reliability, hallucination rate, and latency. The study contributes an open, reproducible design for trustworthy conversational heritage interpretation at sites with limited resources.

candidates.title: Calibrating Large Language Model Agents for Cross-Experiment Prediction Through Preference-Weighted Sampling
candidates.abstract: Using DeepSeek-v4-flash, this study replicates social-preference calibration in the single-stage allocation games examined by Horton and colleagues. The paper estimates sampling weights for three social-preference agent types by constrained least squares and randomly draws agents one by one according to those weights. The paper additionally estimates weights by binomial maximum likelihood using the original human choice counts, and compares the cross-experiment predictions of human choices in two-stage games produced by agents sampled under the two weighting methods. Relative to an unprompted sample, the constrained least-squares calibrated sample reduces prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 51.1% and lowers mean absolute error (MAE) to 0.142833. The binomial-likelihood sample reduces MSE by 51.2%, but its MAE rises to 0.160000, showing no consistent cross-experiment improvement. The error in Berk18 suggests that fixed-preference agents may fail to distinguish game outcomes with equal total payoffs. The results indicate that theory-based social-preference-weighted sampling improves cross-experiment prediction, whereas changing the weight-estimation method alone may be insufficient to resolve errors in agent-behavior prediction.

candidates.title: Rethinking Post-Training Quantization for Large Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large vision-language models (LVLMs) by calibrating quantization parameters on a small dataset without retraining. However, despite increasingly sophisticated calibration strategies, prior methods suffer substantial performance degradation under low-bit weight--activation quantization. To understand this degradation, we locate where quantization error is concentrated and examine the corresponding weight and activation distributions. We observe that a few outliers dominate the ranges shared by per-channel (PC) weights and per-token (PT) activations, leaving insufficient resolution for most values and mapping many of them to zero. These findings motivate a shift in focus from calibration refinement to the underlying quantization representation. We therefore present Rotate-and-Refine Quantization (RRQ) as a simple, effective baseline for LVLM PTQ, combining local Hadamard transforms with group quantization and efficient group-aware execution. Across 8 multimodal tasks and diverse quantization settings, RRQ substantially outperforms baselines while reducing inference time and memory usage. At W4A4, it retains over 96\% of full-precision performance on 8B models and over 99\% on a 32B model, compared with less than 8\% for these baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/kmc3661/RRQ

candidates.title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation
candidates.abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.

candidates.title: Weight-Space Programming with Large Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses a large language model (LLM), often as a coding agent, to read, write or edit another neural network's weights directly, without training it. After a November 2026 MIT CSAIL blog post showed a frontier LLM raising a small model's math score from 8% to 48% by editing its weights, 70 reports followed within three weeks, whose different setups and controls make claims hard to compare. This survey reviews these first 70 reports, including 54 primary studies, and links every extracted claim to a verbatim passage in its source. It distinguishes WSP from fine-tuning, model editing, activation steering, weight-space learning and LLM-as-optimizer methods; proposes a four-axis taxonomy (operation, protocol, mechanism and scope); maps 11 application areas; and audits the controls, baselines and failure modes behind the claims. Three findings emerge. First, LLMs can write small networks from scratch when the task has a short program. Second, apparent reading of weights often rests on surface cues. Third, many reported repairs are simple: a simpler method matched the LLM on at least one task in 34 of 54 primary studies, WSP beat its strongest simple comparator in only 4, and only 13 tested a fix that changes no weights. In a controlled case study of the original MIT repair, the edit gives a real gain, but switching off thinking mode, which changes no weights, recovers 94% of it with 36% of the edited model's tokens; fine-tuning on a larger model's solutions recovers 86%. The survey closes with WSP-12, a twelve-item reporting checklist, and open problems; the coded corpus is public.

candidates.title: Rethinking Reasoning Effort Training in Large Language Models: On-Policy Distillation or Reinforcement Learning?
candidates.abstract: Large language models have shown strong capabilities on complex tasks, yet how to control their reasoning effort remains a significant challenge for practical deployment. This paper provides a systematic investigation of reasoning-effort training, contrasting reinforcement learning (RL) with on-policy distillation (OPD). We find that compressing reasoning and separating effort tiers are governed by different signals. Length-penalized RL reliably compresses a single policy, reducing thinking on AIME25 by 70\% without accuracy loss, but collapses the tiers when they are trained jointly. Multi-teacher OPD separates them: across 33 benchmarks, low and medium use 58\% and 43\% fewer thinking tokens than high, while high improves on the reference policy by 3.1 points. We trace this difference to the training signal. A sequence-level reward cannot tell tier-specific behavior from shared behavior, whereas OPD supplies a tier-specific target at every visited state, including the decision to stop. Building on this analysis, we show that a single token-level KL anchor on the high tier is sufficient to learn separated tiers within one RL stage, and that natural-language effort instructions make this separation emerge from the start of training, yielding a policy competitive with multi-teacher OPD at matched thinking length. Finally, the separation built by dense targets holds only on the states seen in training: it does not carry over to unseen agentic tasks, where effort acts mainly through the number of interaction turns, whereas the compression induced by sequence-level rewards does.

candidates.title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is the mainstream technology to improve the mathematical reasoning ability of large language models, but evaluation protocols across papers are not unified, and low-sampling and high-sampling pass@k metrics often yield inconsistent conclusions, and there is a lack of systematic review of the evaluation practice. Focusing on the core issue of evaluation completeness, this paper systematically combs three RLVR technical routes: outcome supervision, process supervision, and verifier-free, analyzes the principles of representative algorithms, summarizes the experimental results of public papers, and designs a structured coding scheme covering 9 fields. The 9 representative papers are coded one by one from the aspects of technical route, base model, sampling scale, and training configuration. Statistics show that the current RLVR field is deeply in the dilemma of fragmentation of evaluation protocols: the caliber of evaluation indicators is incompatible with each other, high-sampling evaluation data are scarce, and there are obvious differences on whether low sampling can expand the reasoning boundary. The disclosure of key hyperparameters such as temperature and KL coefficient is scattered and unsystematic, and the horizontal comparison lacks a common foundation. Based on this, this paper proposes a structured coding analysis framework to provide a unified benchmark for the horizontal comparison of evaluation results for subsequent research.

candidates.title: Q-Zoom: Query-Aware Adaptive Perception for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require high-resolution visual inputs for fine-grained tasks like document understanding and dense scene perception. However, current global resolution scaling paradigms indiscriminately flood the quadratic self-attention mechanism with visually redundant tokens, severely bottlenecking inference throughput while ignoring spatial sparsity and query intent. To overcome this, we propose Q-Zoom, a query-aware adaptive high-resolution perception framework that operates in an efficient coarse-to-fine manner. First, a lightweight Dynamic Gating Network adaptively bypasses high-resolution processing when coarse global features suffice. Second, for queries demanding fine-grained perception, a Self-Distilled Region Proposal Network (SD-RPN) localizes the task-relevant Region-of-Interest (RoI) directly from intermediate feature spaces. To optimize these modules efficiently, the gating network uses a consistency-aware generation strategy to derive routing labels, while the SD-RPN employs a fully self-supervised distillation paradigm. A continuous spatio-temporal alignment scheme and targeted fine-tuning then fuse the dense local RoI with the coarse global layout. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Q-Zoom establishes a new Pareto frontier. Using Qwen2.5-VL-7B as a primary testbed, Q-Zoom accelerates inference by $2.5\times$ on Document & OCR benchmarks and $4.7\times$ in High-Resolution scenarios in accuracy-matched comparisons against the baseline's peak-accuracy token budget. Furthermore, at its largest visual-token budget, Q-Zoom surpasses the baseline's peak performance by 1.1% and 8.1% on these respective benchmarks, while keeping about $0.8\times$ of the base model's throughput at a matched token budget. These robust improvements transfer consistently to LLaVA, Qwen3-VL, encoder-free Gemma-4, and RL-based thinking-with-image models.

candidates.title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Construction Safety Inspection
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have drawn more research interest in construction safety inspection recently due to their capacity to integrate visual understanding, language understanding, and reasoning. In this paper, a survey is conducted to review the recent research on MLLMs in construction safety inspection, covering techniques, datasets, evaluation, applications, and limitations. The current studies primarily utilize prompt-based adaptation and in-context learning, domain-specific fine-tuning, and knowledge-augmented reasoning to enhance the performance of MLLMs in the construction domain. Applications of MLLMs in construction safety inspection include hazard detection and localization, safety inspection, visual question answering, assistance, and report generation. From the current studies, it can be found that MLLMs can be used to perform flexible and interpretable analysis for construction safety inspection with the assistance of domain knowledge and prompts. Nevertheless, the limitations of MLLMs in construction safety inspection are still present, such as poor visual grounding and spatial reasoning, lack of domain knowledge, lack of large and balanced datasets, and uncertainty of application in real-world scenarios. For the future work, it is recommended to enhance multimodal grounding, construct a larger and more balanced dataset in the construction domain, integrate safety regulations in a trustworthy manner, and perform human validation systematically. MLLMs have great potential to be applied in construction safety inspection; however, they can be used as decision aids rather than replacements for safety inspectors at present.

candidates.title: Legal Natural Language Processing in the Era of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Law is a discipline grounded in language, and the exponential growth of legal documentation spanning judicial decisions, legislation, contracts, and compliance material has made the manual review and analysis of legal text increasingly impractical. Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a natural solution to this challenge, yet effective deployment in specialised domains requires careful adaptation to their distinct terminology, conventions, and reasoning patterns. This thesis investigates the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) and related NLP techniques to the legal domain, with a focus on tasks that are both practically significant and underexplored in the literature. The thesis makes ten contributions across four main areas. First, it surveys and catalogues European case law databases, examining their accessibility, data formats, and regulatory considerations. Second, it examines legal information extraction, compiling a comprehensive corpus of datasets and methods covering named entity recognition, relationship extraction, and event detection, and systematically evaluating LLMs across these tasks. Third, it addresses legal judgment prediction, introducing the first UK Supreme Court judgment prediction dataset and evaluating LLMs on both prediction and legal reasoning generation, including an extension to the Spanish Supreme Court. Fourth, it tackles legal case retrieval, creating the first UK case retrieval dataset at both document and paragraph levels and benchmarking LLM-based embedding models on this task. The thesis concludes with an ethical analysis of using LLMs for legal advice, presenting a global survey of supreme court data availability and examining the implications of knowledge gaps in LLM training data. Collectively, the findings reveal that while LLMs demonstrate considerable promise across legal NLP tasks, significant challenges remain in legal reasoning, multilingual performance, dataset coverage, and evaluation methodology. This work contributes datasets, benchmarks, and empirical insights to support the continued development of responsible and effective legal NLP systems.

candidates.title: Evaluating Latent Knowledge Stability in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.

candidates.title: DO LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS LEARN FROM THEIR MISTAKES?
candidates.abstract: Do Large Language Models Learn from Their Mistakes? investigates whether LLMs genuinely improve after receiving feedback or simply revise their responses within the current conversation. It proposes a trajectory-level evaluation across mathematics, code repair, evidence-grounded question answering, and instruction following, measuring correction success, recurring errors, regressions, overcorrection, acceptance of false feedback, and transfer to new tasks. The study compares six feedback conditions—from self-critique and vague feedback to verified corrections and deliberately incorrect feedback—to distinguish in-context adaptation from persistent memory and actual parameter learning. It is a proposed experimental study, not yet an empirically completed research project.

candidates.title: Beyond Language Form: Semantic Understanding in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The rapid development of large language models has led to a profound and challenging question: is it enough to prove that these models understand the meanings of language if they perform well in linguistic tasks? This paper argues that the success of the task alone does not fully demonstrate its complete semantic understanding ability. Based on the analysis of the distinction between linguistic form and meaning proposed by Bender and Koller and the evidence of statistical shortcuts, this paper explores why successful task performance does not necessarily demonstrate semantic understanding. However, since human-produced text reflects interactions with the world, models trained based on such data might develop conceptual relations and even reference connections through human language practices. Nevertheless, these abilities are still not enough to constitute a complete understanding. In this way, semantic understanding should be regarded as a multidimensional structure, covering conceptual relations, reference, contextual interpretation, and communicative intention. Each of those dimensions should be assessed separately through tests that exclude surface-level shortcuts, rather than inferred from overall task accuracy. The resulting question is which aspects of semantic understanding language models can demonstrate, and what evidence would be needed to assess each of them.

candidates.title: A Survey on Large Language Model-Based Game Agents
candidates.abstract: Game environments provide rich, controllable settings that simulate many aspects of real-world complexity. As such, game agents offer a valuable testbed for exploring capabilities relevant to Artificial General Intelligence [145]. Recently, the emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) provides new opportunities to endow these agents with generalizable reasoning, memory, and adaptability in complex game environments. This survey offers an up-to-date review of LLM-based game agents (LLMGAs) through a unified reference architecture. At the single-agent level, we synthesize existing studies around three core components: memory, reasoning, and perception–action interfaces, which jointly characterize how language enables agents to perceive, think, and act. At the multi-agent level, we outline how communication protocols and organizational models support coordination, role differentiation, and large-scale social behaviors. To contextualize these designs, we introduce a challenge-centered taxonomy linking six major game genres to their dominant agent requirements, from low-latency response in action games to open-ended goal formation in sandbox worlds. An extended version is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02039, with a curated list of related papers continuously updated at https://github.com/git-disl/awesome-LLM-game-agent-papers.

candidates.title: Visual sequence structure shapes in-context choices in vision–language models
candidates.abstract: Vision–language models (VLMs) process ordered images, yet how unlabelled visual context shapes their subsequent choices remains unclear. Using paradigms adapted from human visual statistical learning, we tested three commercial VLM deployments across five experiments without task-specific weight updates. Structured image sequences increased target choices relative to frequency-matched shuffled sequences in two deployments, although invalid responses in the third prevented the preregistered pooled test. Target choices also increased with successor strength. All three deployments preferred previously encountered image orders. Crucially, reversing image order within three-image chunks reduced forward-order choices from 98.7% to 1.9%, with the test question and alternatives unchanged. However, choices involving unseen exemplars of familiar visual categories varied markedly across deployments. These findings show that unlabelled visual sequence structure can systematically influence VLM choices, and underscore the importance of visual context history for understanding and evaluating multimodal models.

candidates.title: Lost on Campus: Evaluating Embodied Spatial Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in the Wild
candidates.abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.

candidates.title: EM-Claw: An Experience-Grounded Language-Model Agent for Auto Cryo-EM Single-Particle Analysis
candidates.abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) processing remains strongly dependent on expert judgement because difficult specimens often require dataset-specific strategies that cannot be captured by a fixed pipeline. Here we present EM-Claw, an experience-grounded multi-agent system for adaptive cryo-EM single-particle analysis. Rather than following a predefined workflow, EM-Claw retrieves processing precedents from previously solved datasets, consults external guidance, proposes and independently evaluates alternative strategies, executes CryoSPARC or RELION jobs, and revises the processing route according to quantitative and visual evidence. Human expertise can be introduced at any stage through natural-language instructions, while successful decisions and processing trajectories are retained as reusable experience. We evaluated EM-Claw on both publicly available cryo-EM datasets and experimental datasets collected in our laboratory, spanning soluble proteins, membrane proteins, GPCR complexes and small transporter monomers. Across these cases, EM-Claw adapted its processing strategies to specimen-specific challenges, including compositional heterogeneity, complex flexibility, preferred orientation and weak particle features. It produced reconstructions at higher resolution than previously published results (0.1~1.3 angstroms improvement) or solved structures that are now being prepared for publication, with no or little human intervention, thereby substantially reducing the time, effort and field experience required for human decision-making.

candidates.title: Closed-form weight edits for long context
candidates.abstract: A language model trained to 65,536 tokens is given the long-context ability of a sibling model trained to 262,144 tokens without gradients and without merging. The paper reports the method first: the context wall is treated as a dynamical system and solved from its source outward, one solved stage after another. It then gives the edits — the content-free position bias of every attention head, re-developed under a new RoPE base in closed form and written into the key projection as a fixed offset; a rank-1 direction and a norm-weight difference taken from the sibling — the per-layer ruler ladder behind the wall, position-gated Dual Chunk Attention, results up to one million tokens, and a paired baseline against the unmodified model. The work continues the weight-space programming of Takehi et al. (2026) at scale: 453 million weights of a 30-billion-parameter model are written without a gradient.

candidates.title: Simultaneous Inference for Watermark Proportions in LLM-Generated Text
candidates.abstract: Watermarking enables detection of text generated by large language models, but practical review also requires quantifying retained signals within content of interest. Readers may choose passages based on their content and refine their selections after examining the watermark evidence. We develop simultaneous lower confidence bounds on the fraction of selected tokens that retain a watermark signal. The bounds hold jointly for the full document and any passages selected during review. We develop structure-adaptive closed testing (SACT), which uses a working model of sequential signal clustering to construct scores for calibrated sign-based tests. Under a conditional null model, the bounds have finite-sample simultaneous validity even when the working model is misspecified. An exact reference-family representation recovers the full closed-testing bounds while enabling efficient repeated queries. In a constructed database-recovery review, SACT detects document-wide watermark signals and provides lower confidence bounds on watermark proportions in selected passages. Assessing related passages together gives a sharper lower bound on their combined signal count. In simulations spanning two watermarking mechanisms and a range of signal strengths and densities, SACT generally has higher power than competing methods.

candidates.title: Governed Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enterprise Compliance and Auditability
candidates.abstract: In enterprise applications, where maintaining high accuracy and contextual relevance is crucial, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has proven to be a promising method for grounding generated content with external knowledge sources to boost performance of Large Language Models (LLMs). The risk of sensitive and regulated data being used in RAG systems increases, making effective governance even more important to ensure compliance, accountability and trust. Nevertheless, the current state of the art of RAG pipelines tends to rely on rather basic approaches that feature transformer-based retrievers and generative models, with little support for access control, provenance or systematic auditing. We call these deficits the Ungoverned RAG Problem, and these pose risks to organizations including data leakage, unverifiable outputs of models, and regulatory compliance. To tackle these challenges, we are introducing a Governed RAG Framework, combining retrieval with policies, extensive metadata management, and end-to-end logging of RAG activities. The proposed framework provides fine-grained access control, maintains information provenance, and supports the generation of the information in a traceable and accountable manner, while not compromising system performance. We show that our approach corrects factual information by 14.7%, minimizes unauthorized data access by 31.2%, and achieves a higher coverage of 96.9% traceability of the responses compared to conventional RAG systems, with similar response time.

candidates.title: Learning Heterogeneous Reasoning in Large Language Models: From Mode Compatibility to Local Bottlenecks
candidates.abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B--14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining \emph{Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs)}, and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.

candidates.title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Homogeneous Academic Documents
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factual reliability of large language models by combining generative capabilities with external knowledge retrieval. While extensively studied in open-domain and heterogeneous corpora, RAG’s performance in highly homogeneous and structured domains, such as institutional academic documents, remains underexplored. These document types are often lengthy, redundant, and formatted according to rigid institutional standards, posing unique challenges for information retrieval and semantic segmentation. This study systematically evaluates chunking strategies for RAG pipelines applied to Indonesian higher education documents, including curricula, syllabi, academic guidelines, and standard operating procedures. We compare fixed-length token-based chunking with varying sizes and overlaps to structure-based chunking aligned with logical document sections. All documents were preprocessed, embedded using IndoBERT-based sentence transformers, and indexed in ChromaDB. Retrieval effectiveness was assessed using Precision@k, Recall@k, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) with curated academic queries. Results indicate that smaller fixed-length chunks achieve higher top-1 precision, whereas structure-based chunks maintain semantic coherence and deliver superior recall across top-k retrieval. Integrating these retrieval strategies with LLaMA 3.2 and a Telegram bot demonstrates practical usability, providing accurate, context-grounded responses in real time. These findings highlight the critical role of chunking and top-k selection in optimizing RAG performance for structured, redundant academic corpora and offer guidance for designing knowledge management systems in higher education.

candidates.title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.

candidates.title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

candidates.title: Test-Time Latent Computation to Improve Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Recent work on Large Language Models (LLMs) suggests that reasoning capabilities can be enhanced at test time not only through longer token-level reasoning traces, but also through additional computation in latent space. This raises a natural question for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): can additional computation in latent space improve visual perception at test time? In this work, we first verify that MLLMs contain stable reusable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting normal generation. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{Lo}ok \textbf{Ba}ck in the \textbf{L}atent \textbf{S}pace (\textbf{Lobals}), a training-free decoding method that identifies the contiguous layer window with the strongest visual-token attention and re-forwards through it, allowing the model to revisit visual evidence in latent space. We demonstrate that this latent-space revisit strategy can improve MLLMs' performance across diverse multimodal settings, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks.

candidates.title: Retrieval-augmented generation for engineering knowledge
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds a language model’s answers in your own documents, so the model reasons over retrieved passages rather than its parametric memory. This chapter explains the full pipeline and where engineering judgement enters it. It starts with the lightweight tools that let you experience grounded artificial intelligence (AI) in minutes, then works through the parts that decide quality at scale: parsing documents (including tables and scanned drawings) without mangling them, chunking so that related content and its context stay together, choosing between vector search, keyword search (BM25) and hybrid retrieval, and adding a knowledge graph when the answer lies in the relationships between documents rather than in any one of them. It treats chunking and parsing as engineering work that needs domain knowledge, not software configuration. The chapter ends with the seven ways RAG systems fail in safety-critical contexts and why ‘eliminates hallucination’ is a claim to interrogate, not accept. By the end you will be able to design, build and critically evaluate a RAG system for engineering knowledge.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. It treats indexing and orchestration as first-class components and agentic workflows as a paradigm of their own, and it covers the agentic work that has appeared since those reviews. Beyond these components, it covers evaluation, applications, and the questions that remain open for future exploration. From tradition to present and beyond, this work systematically reviews RAG from a perspective of the agentic era.

candidates.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

candidates.title: Research on Theories and Methods of Interpretability in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: In recent years, large language models have made significant progress in various aspects of natural language processing due to their powerful language understanding and generation capabilities. However, their internal decision-making processes are highly complex and typically "black-box" in nature, which limits their widespread application in fields such as healthcare, finance, and law. This paper primarily discusses the interpretability issue of large language models. First, we define the concept and scope of interpretability from three perspectives: model transparency, comprehensibility, and trustworthiness, while summarizing the challenges faced in interpretability research—such as massive parameter scale, strong emergent abilities, and complex attention mechanisms. Second, based on different approaches, existing interpretability methods are categorized into three types: mechanism-based methods (e.g., attention visualization, neuron activation analysis, circuit discovery), probe-based methods (e.g., linear probes, causal probes), and generation-based explanation methods (e.g., chain-of-thought prompting, self-explanation generation). We introduce the principles, advantages, and limitations of each category. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between interpretability and model performance, safety, and fairness, arguing that enhancing interpretability can effectively detect model biases, prevent hallucinatory outputs, and increase user confidence. Finally, addressing current research issues such as inconsistent evaluation criteria, difficulty in ensuring explanation fidelity, and limited cross-modal interpretability studies, we propose future research directions—including building causal reasoning frameworks, establishing unified standards, and exploring human-machine collaborative explanation—to advance the field of large language model interpretability.

candidates.title: Multimodal Evaluation of Mesiodens Treatment Planning by Large Language Models and Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons: A Retrospective Comparative Study
candidates.abstract: Introduction and Aims Mesiodens management requires balancing early removal against the risk of injury to developing teeth, and the timing of intervention remains controversial. Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have been primarily evaluated against fixed diagnostic labels rather than preference-sensitive treatment decisions. In this study, we compared mesiodens management decisions generated by multimodal LLMs under Korean and English prompting conditions with those of human experts. Methods This retrospective study included 140 cases (100 cases with 1 mesiodens, 40 cases with 2 mesiodentes) assessed using demographics, orthodontic treatment intent, and radiographs. Three experts independently selected a management decision, and an expert-derived comparator was defined by majority voting or the median ordinal decision. GPT-5.5 Thinking and Gemini 3.1 Pro received identical materials; Korean prompts were repeated 5 times per case and English prompts once. For the exploratory prompting-language comparison, the first Korean evaluation was compared directly with the single English evaluation on a one-to-one basis, whereas all 5 Korean evaluations were retained for repeated-session stability and derivation of the aggregated Korean decision. Agreement was assessed using kappa statistics, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), paired marginal-distribution tests, and mixed-effects regression. Results Inter-expert Fleiss' kappa was 0.506 and 0.532. LLM–comparator agreement was 55.0%-62.0% (1 mesiodens; kappa, 0.127-0.166) and 32.5%-37.5% (2 mesiodentes; weighted kappa, −0.216 to 0.202). In exploratory one-to-one prompting-language comparisons, exact agreement between Korean run 1 and the single English evaluation was 62.0%-63.0% in cases with 1 mesiodens and 52.5%-65.0% in cases with 2 mesiodentes, with model- and task-dependent differences in decision distributions. Repeated Korean sessions were unanimous in 37.0%-38.0% of cases with 1 mesiodens; within-case agreement in cases with 2 mesiodentes was 81.0% (GPT) versus 62.8% (Gemini). Adding LLMs to the expert rater set lowered ICC from 0.513 to 0.278 and 0.654 to 0.158. Orthodontic treatment intent was most strongly associated with intervention-oriented decisions (odds ratio, 34.27 and 11.96; both P < .001). Conclusion Current multimodal LLMs showed limited concordance with the expert-derived comparator, particularly in ordinal 2-mesiodens tasks. Their inclusion was associated with lower overall inter-rater agreement. Clinical Relevance Multimodal LLMs should not be used autonomously for mesiodens treatment planning; adjunctive use requires specialist oversight, repeated output assessment, and prospective outcome-based validation.

candidates.title: Hallucination in multimodal large language models: a comprehensive review of causes, detection, and mitigation
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities by integrating visual perception with natural language reasoning, enabling deployment in high-stakes applications including medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, and scientific document analysis. Yet widespread adoption is significantly impeded by hallucination, the generation of content that is factually incorrect, visually inconsistent, or semantically unfaithful to the provided visual input. Unlike hallucination in purely textual language models, multimodal hallucination encompasses qualitatively distinct failure patterns arising from complex cross-modal interactions between visual encoders, projection layers, and language decoders. This survey provides a comprehensive review of hallucination in MLLMs, synthesising 261 peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2026, of which 114 are directly cited in the manuscript and the remainder informed the systematic synthesis. We introduce a unified six-category taxonomy distinguishing object, attribute, spatial relation, action/event, temporal, and cross-modal inconsistency hallucinations. We systematically analyse root causes across the full MLLM pipeline and provide a critical evaluation of major benchmarks including CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench, AMBER, HaELM, HallusionBench, and VideoHallucer. Detection methods are reviewed across five paradigms uncertainty-based, consistency-based, knowledge-grounded, training-free, and model-based; and mitigation strategies spanning data curation, architectural improvement, training-time alignment, inference-time correction, and reasoning-based approaches are critically assessed. Domain-specific challenges in medical imaging, remote sensing, autonomous driving, and industrial inspection are examined, revealing critical gaps in current evaluation and mitigation practice. The survey concludes with a structured research roadmap identifying six priority directions for 2025–2028, providing an actionable agenda for the community.

candidates.title: Assessing the Classification Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models in Endodontic Case Difficulty Assessment
candidates.abstract: This study evaluated the multimodal capability of ChatGPT-5 Plus and Claude Opus 4.1 in grading endodontic case difficulty according to American Association of Endodontists (AAE) guidelines. A total of 86 cases were curated to establish a reference standard (RS). Cases were categorized into low, moderate, and high difficulty and presented to both models using a standardized prompt. Diagnostic accuracy was calculated, and Cohen's κ assessed agreement with the RS. McNemar's test evaluated differences in model performance, while Fleiss κ assessed short-term repeatability. ChatGPT-5 Plus demonstrated numerically higher accuracy and agreement with the RS than Claude Opus 4.1 across both modalities. McNemar's test showed significant disagreement between each model and the RS (p < 0.001), although inter-model differences were not significant. Short-term repeatability was stable for ChatGPT-5 Plus, whereas Claude Opus 4.1 showed variable repeatability, particularly for radiographic cases. Overall, current multimodal LLMs showed limited capability for endodontic case-difficulty assessment.

candidates.title: An Overview of Large Language Models and Fundamental Algorithms
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are Transformer-based sequence models trained at scale to predict or reconstruct tokens from large corpora. This chapter provides a breadth-first overview of LLMs and the foundational algorithms that dominate their computational profile. It introduces common model families, training objectives, alignment workflows, and evaluation considerations, then connects these concepts to core building blocks such as self-attention, feed-forward sublayers, Mixture-of-Experts routing, and representative compression techniques. The chapter closes by previewing system-level optimizations for training and inference, including parallelism, memory management, KV caching, batching, and serving architectures, which shape cost and performance in practical deployments.

candidates.title: A Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Model for Power System Security Risk Reasoning
candidates.abstract: With the increasing complexity of modern power systems caused by renewable energy integration, distributed energy resources, and cyber–physical interactions, accurate and trustworthy security risk reasoning has become increasingly important. Existing data-driven methods mainly focus on risk prediction based on statistical correlations, while lacking the capability to model causal risk evolution and generate interpretable explanations. This paper proposes a knowledge-augmented large language model framework for power system security risk reasoning (KALLM-PSR). The proposed framework integrates structured power system knowledge with large language model reasoning capabilities to construct knowledge-enhanced representations, perform multi-stage risk propagation analysis, and generate reliability-aware explanations. A consistency evaluation mechanism is further introduced to improve the trustworthiness of reasoning results. Extensive experiments on IEEE 14-bus, 39-bus, and 118-bus systems demonstrate that KALLM-PSR outperforms conventional deep learning models, general large language models (LLMs), and retrieval-augmented approaches in risk identification accuracy, reasoning consistency, explanation quality, and robustness under disturbance conditions. The proposed framework provides an effective approach for intelligent and trustworthy power system security management.

candidates.title: Scalable Inference Acceleration System for LLMs
candidates.abstract: From natural language processing to scientific computing and code assistance, large language models (LLMs) have rapidly moved from research prototypes to widely deployed AI systems. Today, they are widely viewed as foundational models driving the current wave of artificial intelligence. However, as model parameter scales and context lengths continue to grow, LLM inference faces unprecedented challenges in terms of storage capacity and computational intensity. The limited on-chip storage, memory bandwidth, and computing resources of a single accelerator become major bottlenecks as LLM inference scales toward low latency, high throughput, and high energy efficiency. To address these bottlenecks, building inference acceleration clusters composed of multiple nodes has become an important way to support the deployment of large models. However, the inference process in a multi-node environment introduces complex parallel partitioning, cross-device communication, and synchronization overhead. Efficient inference while ensuring scalability remains a key challenge in current system design. This chapter focuses on the customization and optimization of multi-node LLM inference acceleration systems. First, it summarizes typical problem scenarios and related research progress in multi-node LLM inference, and then provides an overview of methods for scalable inference systems from a holistic perspective. Based on this, it discusses parallel strategies on the algorithm side and optimization on the architecture side. Finally, the experimental results and design trade-offs of existing representative systems are analyzed and summarized.

candidates.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

candidates.title: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination
candidates.abstract: Existing methods for assessing training data contamination in Large Language Models achieve high accuracy, but fundamentally rely on gray-box access, rendering them inapplicable to fully black-box environments. This limitation forces auditors to rely on full-sequence sampling or rigid heuristics, both of which incur prohibitive inference costs and struggle to isolate the underlying memorization signal. To overcome this, we propose a generation-based black-box framework that infers context-induced information gain from targeted token discrepancies. We introduce a budget-constrained auditing regime, building on the empirical observation that the membership signal is highly sparse and concentrated in a few highly informative tokens. We formalize this sparsity, showing why uniform sampling needs many more samples than a policy that targets informative positions. Empirically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art black-box separation accuracy while needing about 3x fewer queries than uniform position sampling. Finally, we apply this methodology to closed frontier models, exploring its capacity and limits in surfacing potential training data overlaps on commercial APIs.

candidates.title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
candidates.abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias. We investigate decision models (System One architectures) for silicon sampling. Using choice training, we update KEV model weights on historical respondent-level choice microdata by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without target-study data. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies from new domains (vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights, and AI) and new response formats. A small choice-trained model outperforms a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies. Although training on single studies lowers cross-entropy, it can exacerbate treatment-effect error. Choice training thus complements post-inference calibration by providing a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences.
