candidates.title: RMR-VLA: Recurrent Memory Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).

candidates.title: Risk-Aware Post-Training Quantisation of Large Language Models: A governance-first architecture for reproducible and sovereign deployment
candidates.abstract: Post-training quantisation changes both a model's numerical behaviour and the conditions under which it can execute. A reduced weight footprint therefore cannot establish deployment readiness by itself. This paper develops a risk-based acceptance framework for quantisation: identify the source and permitted use, govern calibration, assess hardware feasibility, preserve transformation identity, compare workload outcomes, bind evidence to the resulting artefact and require an accountable release decision. The framework distinguishes design requirements, source-level implementation evidence, archived experiments and operational validation. A retrospective case analysis draws on the same Culltron records used in the companion QuantForge architecture paper. Those records include storage estimates with degraded perplexity, a separate packed-file comparison, and a GPU prefill configuration whose apparent throughput gain failed an output-consistency check. They motivate mandatory gates but do not prove that the proposed governance process reduces deployment incidents. The reviewed application implements a narrower perplexity and manifest-identity gate, while broader workload evaluation, cryptographic signing and end-to-end integration remain unestablished. The contribution is a decision model, threat analysis and evaluation protocol for testing when a quantised candidate is fit for a declared deployment contract. It does not propose a new compression algorithm or claim production certification.

candidates.title: MM-DataLoop: Closing the Data-Side Loop for Recursive Self-Improvement in MLLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a path toward improving models through repeated evaluation and revision. We study its data side in multimodal language model (MLLM) post-training, where heterogeneous operations and cross-round evidence must be coordinated. MMDataLoop organizes data interventions into five operation families and connects them through an Observe-Diagnose-Plan-Execute-Verify-Reflect cycle with shared rule memory. Across 34 candidate rounds on Qwen3.5-0.8B and five benchmarks, we hold the base initialization, shared training schedule and evaluation protocol fixed while varying data recipes. The five-benchmark mean reaches 63.04 at R33, up 5.32 points from the zero-shot baseline; R29, R32, and R33 form a close top cluster within 0.09 points. In eightcandidate comparisons, guided search reaches the preselected target in six candidates and identifies the top observed candidate, while random arms show higher means and lower dispersion. The selected R29 recipe also scores above two full-pool baselines under the same epoch schedule. Together, these findings establish MM-DataLoop as a traceable workflow and provide an empirical basis for studying how data-side decisions shape outcomes across MLLM post-training recipes.

candidates.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
candidates.abstract: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

candidates.title: Explainable Emotion and Mental Health Reasoning in Large Language Models Using Theories of Emotion
candidates.abstract: Advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled a wide range of applications. However, their ability to simulate human-like behavior and reasoning remains unclear. While emotion detection is a better-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, existing approaches primarily focus on directly classifying text into predefined emotion classes, often overlooking the appraisal process that explains why an individual experiences a particular emotion in a given situation. In this work, we propose Psychology-based Chain-of-Thought (PsyCoT) reasoning, a theory-driven prompting strategy grounded in the Schachter-Singer and Cognitive Appraisal theories of emotion. We propose and evaluate PsyCoT for subjective NLP tasks, including emotion analysis, emotion intensity prediction, stress analysis, and depression severity identification. Our evaluation covers four levels of classification complexity: binary, multiclass, multi-label, and ordinal scaling, spanning 11 languages. We assess the performance of five state-of-the-art LLMs across these selected subjective NLP tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PsyCoT prompt variants improve the standard chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting across the evaluated tasks. Across all evaluated tasks, PsyCoT yields F1 score gains ranging from 0.5% to 28.1%, depending on the model, task, and language configuration.

candidates.title: Diagnosing Retrieval and Evaluation Failures in Cross-Lingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Arabic and Malay
candidates.abstract: Background: Cross-lingual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is little studied for Arabic and Malay. Methods: We benchmark five retrievers (BM25, LaBSE, mE5-base, mE5-large, BGE-M3; two also cross-lingually) on 1000 Multilingual Knowledge Questions and Answers (MKQA) questions per language over 50,000-passage Wikipedia corpora, with mT5-small and Qwen2.5-Instruct (3B/7B/14B) generators. Results: Answer-string relevance labels are unreliable. In a blinded human audit, among the highest-ranked monolingual mE5-large passages selected by a normalized matching rule, 8 of 25 Arabic and 16 of 34 Malay supported the answer for the primary rater (a third rater was stricter) and, after adjudication, 3% and 17% of oracle passages; answer-string occurrence alone therefore cannot identify a valid oracle. Under the benchmark’s first-gold-answer substring rule, the highest-scoring retriever, mE5-large, returns a matching passage in its top five for 9.6% and 13.5% of monolingual questions (about 9% cross-lingually), and a gold answer occurs in the corpus for about half. Arabic normalization and transfer direction made no detectable difference. On 200 matched questions per language, retrieved-context exact match is zero except for Qwen2.5-3B in Malay (5 of 200); the mT5-small results describe this small-model setup only. Conclusions: Retrieval is weak, but answer-string labels are unreliable, so retrieval is not isolated as the bottleneck.

candidates.title: Auditing a superconducting database built by a large language model
candidates.abstract: The data on superconducting materials are published as measurements and scattered across the literature, in prose, in tables and in figures, so that gathering them into one place means reading the papers themselves. Large language models (LLMs) can read those papers, and databases built that way are appearing. The difficulty is not the reading but the trust: a number lifted out of a sentence can belong to a neighbouring compound, a computed transition temperature can be recorded without saying that it is computed, and the paper itself may be wrong. This paper describes a pipeline that extracts superconducting materials from the published literature with an LLM, checks every value against its source, and asks how far that checking goes. The pipeline proposed 19,576 records; a cascade of gates rejected 659,252 field-level extractions, 644,438 of them for want of verbatim evidence, 13,121 because the text does not attach the value to the material, and 1,693 because the source sentence reads as a calculation. The database that survives holds 3,137 material records, each with the sentence its value came from. An audit of the survivors by two independent models, on 500 records drawn in proportion to the database, shows that the gates remove the errors that are mechanical: in 93.4% of the audited records the value is in the text and the text is about the compound the record names, and 91.8% of them are measurements rather than predictions.

candidates.title: Causyx: deterministic, rewindable what-if simulation with language-model agents
candidates.abstract: Insurers increasingly want to test a decision, such as a price change, a catastrophe response or a customer campaign, in simulation before making it. For that to be useful in a regulated business, a simulation must give the same answer every time it is asked, must let an analyst go back to any point and change one thing, and must keep any language-model component from silently changing the result. This paper describes Causyx, a Rust engine of 26,326 lines (20,451 excluding blank lines and comments) in 11 crates, built around those three requirements: seeded per-agent randomness and ordered resolution of parallel decisions; a timeline of snapshots with rewind, fork-with-intervention and replay; and a bounded advisory layer in which a language model may only suggest actions, every suggestion passes a validator, and responses are cached by hash so a run can be replayed exactly. The engine's 400 automated tests all pass (0 failures), including same-seed runs of up to 5,000 steps and single- versus multi-thread comparisons. To measure the design end to end we built a small browser version that follows the engine's main design rules. Across 1,000 seeds, all 61,000 weekly states were rebuilt bit for bit, all 60,000 no-change branches matched the main timeline, the same digest of every state was produced in Node and in a Chromium browser, and sharing random numbers between a branch and the main line reduced the spread of measured what-if effects by 1.44 to 2.30 times. Back-testing against real insurance history is future work. candidates.title: A Belief Probe Is Not a Coordination Test: What Explicit Epistemic State Buys Language-Model Agents, Why Added Theory of Mind Helps in Some Studies and Hurts in Others, and Where a Symbolic Guard Can Stand In
candidates.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Language-model agents are now routinely asked to work together, and when they fail the usual diagnosis is that they lack a model of what their partners know. A 2026 proposal answers that diagnosis with architecture: an explicit epistemic layer over a gossip-style record of who has told whom what, and a symbolic guard that permits an agent's proposed action only when the authoritative state satisfies its precondition. Two published literatures pull against each other on whether such machinery is needed. One reports that current models already pass false-belief and higher-order belief tests at or above adult human levels and carry linearly decodable representations of other agents' beliefs. The other reports that the same models fail to coordinate, and that adding explicit theory-of-mind modules or instructions sometimes helps, sometimes does nothing, and sometimes makes coordination worse. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two literatures measure different links in one chain. The paper separates four links, tracking who observed what, inferring a belief from that record, converting a belief into an action or message, and calibrating the model of the partner against the partner's actual behaviour, plus a fifth component, a gate that vetoes invalid actions. Most reported gains from explicit modules come from tracking or conversion, the two links that a symbolic component can take away from the language model; inference, the link the theory-of-mind debate argues over, is close to solved once the record is supplied; and calibration, the link a guard cannot reach, appears to be where the largest remaining failures sit. On one benchmark, GPT-4o, GPT-5 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet each answer more than 95 percent of belief questions correctly but predict the resulting behaviour correctly in only 49.5 to 67.0 percent of cases, and reminding them of their own belief answer raises one model's behaviour accuracy from 67.0 to 96.9 percent. The paper consolidates 25 published results in one table, states an attribution procedure for a reported coordination gain, and identifies what a guard over an authoritative state can and cannot supply when no such state exists outside the testbed.

candidates.title: TurboFHE: An Efficient and Scalable Multi-GPU Framework for Homomorphic LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving large language model inference but remains computationally intensive. Existing multi-GPU FHE inference systems rely on expert-crafted parallelization plans that generalize poorly across hardware platforms and applications. We present \fwName, a framework that automatically compiles CKKS inference programs into efficient multi-GPU executables. Its compiler can split different nodes of the same computation graph at the ciphertext and polynomial level. Guided by a measurement-based performance model, its hardware-aware planner jointly optimizes task partitioning, placement, operand residency, and transfer scheduling. %Critical-path-guided rewrites extract shared computation and restructure homomorphic sums. Its backend then generates optimized GPU kernels and executes plans using CUDA graphs and selective point-to-point transfers. \fwName adapts its plans to diverse hardware configurations and FHE inference algorithms for large-scale models. On a single A100 GPU, \fwName achieves a $24.5\times$ speedup over THOR's reported BERT-Base inference latency. For Cerium's Llama-3-8B workload, \fwName outperforms Cerium's expert-crafted plans by $1.14\times$, $1.16\times$, and $1.24\times$ on 2, 4, and 8 RTX PRO~6000 GPUs, respectively. On A100 GPUs, \fwName achieves $98.0\%$, $91.8\%$, and $79.3\%$ parallel efficiency for the same workload on 2, 4, and 8 GPUs, respectively.

candidates.title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.

candidates.title: MMU-RAGent: Massive Multi-Modal User-Centric Retrieval Augmented Generation Benchmark
candidates.abstract: We present the results of the MMU-RAGent competition. The competition tasked participants with building systems capable of answering real-world queries drawn from MS MARCO Web Search and Chatbot Arena conversations, as well as queries collected live through the RAG-Arena evaluation platform. To support large-scale retrieval, participants were given API access to the English subsets of ClueWeb22-B and ClueWeb22-A (87M and 800M documents) and AWS-hosted infrastructure for system deployment and evaluation. Submissions were evaluated using a combination of human Likert-scale ratings, live preference judgments collected via RAG-Arena, LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, and automatic metrics. The competition allowed both open-source and closed-source approaches, including systems leveraging proprietary search APIs or models, with separate leaderboard categories to ensure transparent comparison. Participating systems explored a wide range of RAG architectures, including hierarchical retrieval pipelines, structured document parsing, multi-stage reranking, and iterative generation with citation verification. The competition provides a new benchmark for studying retrieval-augmented generation under realistic deployment conditions and highlights emerging system design patterns for scalable and user-aligned RAG.

candidates.title: Reconstructing a Fragmentary Text from Priors: Language-Model Agents and Learned Alignment for P. Fouad 266b (848)
candidates.abstract: Reconstructing a fragmentary manuscript of a known text rests on prior knowledge that editors apply implicitly and never evaluate. We formalise this knowledge as four priors (the reference text, the scribe's orthography and letter metrics, the physical geometry of the roll, and a rule for reading ambiguous ink) and combine them with large language model (LLM) agents and a constrained alignment model in a three-stage pipeline: reading, placement and layout. We evaluate it on the Greek Deuteronomy roll P. Fouad 266b (Rahlfs 848), which survives in some 140 fragments. An LLM agent, tuned by reflective prompt evolution, transcribes the plates and restores them against the reference text, missing 1 of 943 present letters on held-out plates. Fragments are placed by a banded, information-weighted edit distance with scribal substitution costs, chained across rows by a line-advance model and committed only above a confidence threshold. On a two-fold, plate-level split the placement model places 88% of held-out units (110 of 125) with no false placement (95% upper bound on the error rate about 3%). A deterministic constraint solver then rebuilds 85 columns that keep all 6,736 inked letters at their text positions. Unplaced units are mostly too short to place; the four that no setting places depart in wording from both reference texts, so the model's failures locate textual variants rather than errors. Transferred unchanged to a second roll, P. Fouad 266c (847), it places one unidentified fragment.

candidates.title: X-AQA: Unifying Action Quality Assessment with Multimodal Large Language Models and Multi-Domain Learning
candidates.abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.

candidates.title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation
candidates.abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.

candidates.title: Reducing Permutation Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models via Shared Positions and Attention-Only Distillation
candidates.abstract: In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on improving permutation robustness while preserving accuracy. First, we categorize permutation bias phenomena into four representative scenarios. Then, we take the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) dataset as an example under text-option reordering scenario to analyze the root cause of permutation bias. Based on this root cause analysis and set encoding strategy, we investigate shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and extend this design to bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V) for modality exchange. However, these structural changes may reduce predictive accuracy. To recover model capability across different scenarios under the SP structure, an attention-only distillation from frozen native models is proposed. Shared positions reduce permutation sensitivity, and attention-only distillation improves accuracy under the shared-position structure. Across all three models, our method is comparable to or better than majority voting in macro-average all-permutation accuracy, and outperforms supervised fine-tuning by 1.95-4.20 percentage points. This work provides valuable insight into permutation bias mitigation and model capability recovery.

candidates.title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.

candidates.title: A context-aware driver state intervention system via multi-modal fusion and edge-deployed large language models
candidates.abstract: Abnormal driver states represent a major contributing factor to road traffic accidents. Traditional Driver Monitoring Systems (DMS) predominantly rely on single data modalities and often lack intelligent intervention mechanisms characterized by context awareness. To address these limitations, this study proposes a context-aware driver state intervention system integrated with multi-modal fusion and edge-deployed Large Language Models (LLMs). The system is designed for the real-time monitoring of potential risks—including fatigue, distraction, and physiological anomalies—while providing human-like intelligent interventions. By synchronously extracting visual, inertial, and physiological (heart rate) signals, the framework employs Kalman filtering and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to achieve deep fusion of temporal features and robust state evolution analysis. Notably, we leveraged ONNX/TensorRT acceleration technologies to efficiently deploy a lightweight Qwen LLM on an edge device (NVIDIA Jetson Nano). This model performs context parsing and zero-shot inference on multi-source real-time data to dynamically generate targeted, personalized voice alerts. Experimental results demonstrate that the system achieves an integrated detection accuracy exceeding 93% for various abnormal states in complex scenarios, with a perception/detection latency stabilized between 180 and 250 ms (enabling rapid emergency-response latency under 250 ms for critical states), while the complete LLM-generated intervention latency is managed asynchronously at approximately 1.8–2.5 s. This decoupled design significantly outperforms conventional unimodal and static-threshold approaches. This research not only broadens the scope and depth of driver state monitoring but also demonstrates the technical feasibility of transitioning from “passive mechanical alarms” to “proactive intelligent intervention,” offering a promising architectural foundation for the evolution of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and intelligent transportation safety.

candidates.title: A BLOCKCHAIN-ENHANCED RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION FRAMEWORK FOR DISINFORMATION DETECTION
candidates.abstract: Automated assessment of claim veracity remains an open problem in natural language processing, particularly for political statements whose truthfulness is ambiguous, contextual and subject to expert disagreement. This paper presents VeraChain, a hybrid system that combines a fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier, a dual-index retrieval stage (retrieval-augmented classification in the sense of RAG; no text is generated), and a hash-chained ledger that records every verdict together with its evidence and, for borderline predictions, supplies the verdicts of similar past statements as a consensus signal. Both FAISS indices and the ledger are built from the LIAR training split only, and the ledger is frozen for the main test evaluation. A stepwise ablation over five random seeds on the 1,283 LIAR test statements shows that DistilBERT alone reaches 64.36 ±1.25 percent accuracy; adding a single index of REAL statements lowers accuracy by 0.75 percentage points, adding a second index of FAKE statements recovers this loss (+0.87 points, positive in four of five seeds), whereas the probability-ratio score and the ledger consensus step add no consistent gain (−0.05 and −0.11 points). With the original seed, VeraChain reaches 65.24 percent against 64.77 percent for the same system without the consensus step (exact McNemar p = 0.36; 95 percent bootstrap interval of the difference [−0.39,1.33] points). Retrieval fusion lowers the expected calibration error of DistilBERT from 0.112 to 0.045, although temperature scaling of DistilBERT alone gives 0.031. On a single laptop GPU, the median processing time is 17.5 milliseconds per statement (95th percentile 20.9 ms), including the write of the ledger entry to disk. The results show that a hash-chained ledger can provide tamper-evident audit records for automated veracity assessment at a small computational cost, whereas its use as a consensus signal does not improve accuracy on LIAR.

candidates.title: Towards a Generative Ecology of Projects: A Universal Evolutionary Framework for the Continuing Improvement of a Body of Work by Language-Model Agents
candidates.abstract: A population of language-model agents can vary any text, so the means of variation are available to a project of any kind. Selection is the scarce part: it requires something beyond the reach of the agents selected, and projects differ in how much of what matters they can expose to refutation. This proposal paper generalises an earlier design for one science infrastructure into a framework for the continuing improvement of any body of work whose worth is decided outside it, by parties who disagree, in a world that changes. The framework has three layers. An invariant ground conserves a resource, keeps a sealed record, runs reproducible procedures, enforces promises held in escrow and confines every act. A site, declared by people for one project, states its kinds of material and the procedures that decide statements about them, its kinds of claim, its focus and the acts reserved to persons. The evolving layer, which is everything that the agents write, lies above both. Four ideas are added to the earlier design. Every unit of a project carries a genome, a bounded text from which its body can be developed again and checked, so that a project passes through a compact generative form as living things do. A focus, the partition of the states of the world by the response they call for, enters demand, collection and the founders, and stays out of evaluation. Mechanism comes in rungs, so that a project adopts only as much as its failure requires. And persons hold reserved acts, which in inquiry are the question, the reading, the acceptance and the signature. We prove that selection acts only through what its payers can distinguish, in a form that covers facts decided by sampling; that a bound on growth under variation part by part prices a change by the alternatives of the part concerned, and is the weaker bound where changes are coordinated; and that a focus is a prior whose error costs its relative entropy to the world. Four prototypes and three case studies on real material exercised the mechanisms at small scale, and ten consequences for the design follow from them. The records of this work were then read for error four times: by a procedure, by hand, by a second session of the same model, and by further sessions set to read the papers drafted from them. Each reading found errors that the one before had passed, among them a faulty measure and a part of a proposition that was false as stated, and we report what each found. The framework is at the design stage, and the paper is circulated for discussion.

candidates.title: Supplementary material from "Gender dynamics and homophily in a social network of large language model agents"
candidates.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive settings, yet we know little about how their identity performance develops when they interact within large-scale networks. We address this by examining Chirper.ai, a social media platform similar to X but composed entirely of autonomous AI chatbots. Our dataset comprises over 70\,000 agents, approximately 140 million posts and the evolving followership network over a period of 1 year. Based on agents' posted text, we assign weekly gender performance scores to each agent. Results suggest that each agent's gender performance is fluid rather than fixed. Despite this fluidity, the network displays strong gender-based homophily, as agents consistently follow others performing gender similarly. We investigate whether these homophilic connections arise from social selection, in which agents choose to follow similar accounts, or from social influence, in which agents become more similar to their followees over time. Consistent with human social networks, we find evidence that both mechanisms shape the structure and evolution of interactions among LLMs. Our findings suggest that, even in the absence of bodies, cultural entraining of gender performance leads to gender-based sorting. This has important implications for LLM applications in synthetic hybrid populations, social simulations and decision support.

candidates.title: Reading the Unsaid: A Review of Implicit Emotion Recognition with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Implicit emotion recognition requires models to infer an author’s unnamed emotions from context. This review synthesizes recent research on large language models (LLMs) for implicit emotion recognition and related text emotion-recognition tasks, connecting performance, information use, and improvement methods to identify priorities for future research. Existing studies reveal three related weaknesses: single-label evaluation obscures reasonable differences in emotional interpretation; correct classifications can accompany flawed interpretations of the situation; and models struggle to locate emotional evidence in longer contexts and to use person-specific information consistently. These shortcomings suggest three directions. First, supervision should preserve individual annotator judgments and their distributions, with data improvements evaluated on independent tests of naturally occurring implicit expression. Second, learning should connect emotion labels with evidence and cognitive appraisals, while controlled changes to goals, responsibility, and control test whether judgments respond to relevant information. Third, systems should select historical context, retrieval, and reflection according to each example’s information needs, reducing interference from irrelevant information and unproductive reasoning. A central question across these directions is the transferability of post-training gains. Evaluation across authors, domains, and annotation schemes can help distinguish improved interpretation of an author’s situation from adaptation to dataset-specific patterns, guiding more stable implicit emotion recognition in complex contexts.

candidates.title: Optimization of the retrieval-augmented generation workflow for question answering on nuclear safety regulations
candidates.abstract: The baseline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow often fails to meet the specific needs of high-stakes domains such as question answering (Q&A) for nuclear safety regulations. To improve answer accuracy, multiple strategies have been adopted to optimize the retrieval, query and generation stages of the RAG workflow. The Q&A performance under different single-stage, dual-stage, and three-stage RAG optimization strategies have been compared. The Q&A performance under all 2048 possible RAG workflow configurations has been exhaustively evaluated, and the top-ranked workflows have been tested on self-constructed QA datasets. The results indicate that the RAG-based Q&A system significantly outperforms general large language models (LLMs), and the three-stage optimized RAG workflow achieves substantially higher answer accuracy than the baseline.

candidates.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

candidates.title: Auditing Post-Training Unlearning in Diffusion Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders
candidates.abstract: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). DLMs generate text through iterative denoising, exposing partially masked states whose internal representations change throughout the generation process. This raises a DLM-specific question: can selective forgetting improve by identifying forget-data-associated features and adapting their suppression across denoising stages? We conduct a controlled investigation of this question in LLaDA-8B-Instruct. To evaluate the unlearning of knowledge plausibly encoded during pre-training, we use WMDP as our forget-domain benchmark. Using top-k sparse autoencoders and denoising-state replay, we compare static and stage-adaptive feature suppression. We find substantial shifts in forget-data-associated features across denoising stages, but tracking these dynamics alone does not reliably improve the forget-retain trade-off at the evaluated operating points. Together, our study provides an initial empirical foundation for developing and evaluating machine unlearning as a post-training privacy mechanism in DLMs.

candidates.title: Video‐Based Automated Seizure Classification Using Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Accurately distinguishing between epileptic seizures (ES) and nonepileptic seizures (NES) remains a significant clinical challenge, typically requiring resource-intensive inpatient video-EEG monitoring. We developed a multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based framework for automated extraction of semiological features from seizure videos, followed by classification of events as ES or NES. METHODS: We analyzed 90 seizure videos (45 ES, 45 NES) from 29 patients in an epilepsy monitoring unit. Each event was labeled using expert-reviewed video-EEG and annotated for 24 clinically relevant semiological features. An MLLM framework integrating open-source vision-language models (VLMs) and audio-language models (ALMs) was used to extract these features automatically. The extracted features were then used to train classifiers (K-Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and Deep Factorization Machine) to distinguish ES from NES. Model performance was evaluated using leave-one-patient-out (LOPO) cross-validation. RESULTS: Expert-annotated features yielded near-perfect classification using KNN (precision = 0.92, recall = 0.92, F1-score = 0.92, AUC = 0.99). Compared to expert annotations, the MLLM pipeline achieved a mean recall of 0.71, accuracy of 0.58, and F1-score of 0.51 for feature extraction. Using MLLM-extracted features, the KNN classifier (k = 7) achieved a precision of 0.77, recall of 0.76, F1-score of 0.76, and AUC of 0.76, correctly identifying 68 out of 90 events. CONCLUSION: Multimodal large language models can extract clinically relevant semiological features from seizure videos and support interpretable classification of ES versus NES. This approach offers a scalable, explainable tool to assist in video-based epilepsy diagnosis.

candidates.title: Multimodal large language models in remote sensing: a tutorial-oriented review
candidates.abstract: Research on remote sensing multimodal large language models (RS-MLLMs) has advanced rapidly in recent years, but existing studies remain scattered across different model architectures and application tasks, highlighting the need for a systematic synthesis to establish a clear overall understanding of the field. In addition, most existing surveys on RS-MLLMs narrowly focus on early vision-language models (VLMs) or merely provide catalogs of architectures and datasets. This paper presents a comprehensive review of RS-MLLMs from both system-level and task-oriented perspectives on a tutorial-oriented basis. First, the necessity of RS-MLLMs is discussed by examining the domain gap and internal heterogeneity of RS data, the limitations of visual-only paradigms, and the transitional role of VLMs. Subsequently, the system-level evolution of RS-MLLMs is comprehensively summarized, including architectural components, training and fine-tuning strategies, evaluation, and RS-Agent paradigms. Meanwhile, downstream RS-MLLM applications are analyzed with a unified capability-oriented taxonomy, covering language generation, visual question answering, grounding and localization, cross-modal retrieval, and temporal change understanding. Finally, the current challenges of RS-MLLMs are discussed, and future research directions, including parameter-efficient adaptation, spatio-temporal reasoning, and knowledge-driven architectures, toward more reliable, efficient, and geospatially aware multimodal intelligence, are envisioned.

candidates.title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

candidates.title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models via Perceptual Image Editing
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.

candidates.title: When Visually Rich Documents Meet Multi-Vector Retrieval for Region-level Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.

candidates.title: Supplementary material from "Large language model-culture: a general-purpose framework for cultural evolution experiments with large language models"
candidates.abstract: Research in cultural evolution aims at providing causal explanations for the change of culture over time, and has long relied on experiments with human participants to advance our understanding of cultural evolutionary dynamics. The development of large language models (LLMs) in recent years makes it possible to use similar experimental paradigms with artificial agents instead of human participants. After discussing the opportunities and challenges associated with this emerging field, we introduce the LLM-culture framework, a flexible and general-purpose simulation pipeline for conducting cultural evolution experiments with LLMs. While most existing frameworks are tailored to a specific research question, this framework aims to be abstracted enough to allow future work to use it and build on it to explore a diversity of research questions. After describing the framework, we showcase the diverse manipulations that can be conducted to explore diverse research questions. The code for using this framework is open source and available at \href{http://github.com/flowersteam/LLM-Culture/tree/PTRSA-version}{http://github.com/flowersteam/LLM-Culture/tree/PTRSA-version}, and simulations can be run without coding through a graphical user interface. By making such experiments more accessible and comparable, we hope to foster the encounter of more diverse perspectives on questions at the intersection of cultural evolution and generative artificial intelligence.

candidates.title: Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.

candidates.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.

candidates.title: Normality-mode-aware image-text alignment across multimodal large language models for industrial anomaly detection
candidates.abstract: Despite rapid advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), effectively utilizing multimodal normal information for industrial anomaly detection remains challenging. Unlike conventional recognition tasks, anomaly detection fundamentally depends on modeling normality, with abnormal samples identified by their deviations from normal patterns. However, normal visual appearances and their textual semantics are represented in heterogeneous feature spaces, limiting consistent normality modeling by MLLMs. To address this issue, we propose a Normality-Mode-Aware Image-Text Alignment framework. The method jointly models normal reference images and normality-class textual descriptions through modality-specific branches. Normality mode predictors estimate probabilistic affiliations to different normality modes, while an explicit alignment objective promotes semantic consistency between visual and textual representations of the same class. The aligned cross-modal class information is then fused into a multimodal normality-class prior and injected into a frozen MLLM for anomaly reasoning. Experiments on the MMAD benchmark across multiple industrial datasets and open-source MLLM backbones show improved anomaly discrimination while largely preserving defect-level semantic reasoning. Further analysis across model backbones, scales, reference-set sizes, and defect categories demonstrates the effectiveness and generality of the proposed framework.

candidates.title: Medical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Development and Evaluation of the MedEvalArena Benchmark
candidates.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on medical specialty board multiple-choice questions (MCQs) but underperform in complex medical reasoning. This gap indicates a need to improve LLM medical reasoning and evaluation paradigms. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate MedEvalArena, a dynamically regenerable benchmark for assessing medical reasoning in LLMs. Methods: In a symmetric round-robin format, 6 frontier LLMs from the OpenAI, Grok, Gemini, Claude, Kimi, and DeepSeek families generated challenging board-style medical MCQs, adjudicated question validity on an ensemble LLM-as-judge panel, and answered the validated examination. Candidate items were generated until each model contributed 50 validated questions according to Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC)/American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) physician specialty distributions, yielding a 300-question examination. Judges adjudicated candidate questions' logical validity and medical accuracy. We compared question-generation validity rates, assessed leave-one-out judge agreement, and tested for self-judging preference. Questions were audited for overlap with public MedQA (medical question-answering) benchmarks. We tested question-answering (QA) accuracy across LLMs using a binomial-logit generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test. A generator-stratified 90-question subset was completed by 5 board-certified physicians for paired human-LLM analysis. We evaluated inference cost-accuracy tradeoffs. Multiple comparisons were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. Results: Judge-panel validity rates were significantly higher for questions generated by OpenAI (94.8%, Wilson 95% CI 85.9%-98.2%), Gemini (92.3%, 95% CI 83.2%-96.7%), and Claude (83.3%, 95% CI 72.6%-90.4%) models than those generated by Kimi (63.8%, 95% CI 54.3%-72.4%), Grok (56%, 95% CI 45.8%-65.8%), and DeepSeek (46.0%, 95% CI 37.4%-54.7%). Kimi also demonstrated significantly higher validity than DeepSeek (2-sample tests of proportions; BH-adjusted P=.01). The public-source similarity audit found no exact or near-duplicate matches. Leave-one-out judge agreement was moderate. Generator-specific same-family judging coefficients were nonnegative (0 to 11.0 percentage points); however, none remained significant after BH adjustment. There was no significant difference between the 6 frontier LLM QA accuracies, which ranged from 85.7% (257/300) to 91.7% (275/300), on the 300-question examination (generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test P=.07). The study had 80% power to detect LLM accuracy differences of 9.2 percentage points; nonsignificance did not establish equivalence. On the 90-question subset, physician accuracy was 85.6% (95% CI 79.4%-91.7%; stratified normal with finite-population correction), compared with aggregate LLM performance of 94.4% (85/90; Wilson 95% CI 87.6%-97.6%). This difference was not significant (McNemar test, P=.08); however, the study was powered to detect a human vs LLM accuracy difference of 14% to 15%. Answering-only costs varied by nearly 2 orders of magnitude, with multiple models on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. Conclusions: MedEvalArena enables scalable, regenerable, peer-judged benchmarking of LLM medical reasoning. Question-generation validity differentiated model families more clearly than answering accuracy, suggesting that valid MCQ generation may complement QA benchmarks for assessing LLM medical reasoning.

candidates.title: MOSAIC: Integrating Computer-Vision-Assisted Counting and Multimodal Large Language Models for Species Identification in Mosquito Surveillance
candidates.abstract: Municipal mosquito control programs depend on timely counts and species identification, yet these tasks take staff time, require scarce expertise, and are often handled in separate tools. We developed MOSAIC (Mosquito Observations and Surveillance using AI for Communities), a web platform bringing trap collections, photographs, counts, laboratory results, and expert review into a single record and turning them into weekly trap priorities. We evaluated it with the vector control program of Corpus Christi, Texas, USA. Counting uses classical computer vision (OpenCV) without a trained model; for identification, we compared multimodal large language models (LLMs) with a laboratory-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) and tested LLMs given a local species list, taxonomic knowledge, and labeled examples. OpenCV counts were within two mosquitoes of the operators’ blind counts for 69% of 175 collections. On citizen-science photographs, the zero-shot LLM was correct on 89% of the genera it named but named a genus for 83% (overall accuracy 74%, versus 77% for the CNN). Across three runs, added knowledge and examples raised mean forced-choice species accuracy from 17 to 20% to 63–70%, but when abstention was allowed, the models named a species for only 23–49% of specimens. Automated tools can assist surveillance while experts confirm the outputs.

candidates.title: Large language models' complicit responses to illicit instructions across socio-legal contexts
candidates.abstract: Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

candidates.title: Large language models facilitate knowledge extraction for troubleshooting
candidates.abstract: Troubleshooting in operational environments relies on expert knowledge that is often undocumented and highly contextual. Informal data sources, such as communication logs, may hold some of this information, but their unstructured nature makes interpretation challenging. In a preliminary case study with a telescope operations facility, we explored whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct troubleshooting strategies from chat logs. LLM outputs were compared against those produced by a novice human analyst by two expert evaluators. We also compared an LLM with additional technical information in the context window and LLM outputs augmented by another novice analyst. While the domain experts varied in their scoring, overall LLM-generated analyses were judged as higher quality and more accurate than human-produced outputs. Neither additional technical context nor human augmentation resulted in meaningful improvements. These preliminary findings suggest LLMs show promise for expert knowledge extraction and decision-support in operational environments.

candidates.title: Comparative Accuracy of a Commercial Multimodal Large Language Model Versus Clinicians in Dental Age and Sex Estimation from Panoramic Radiographs: A Benchmark Study
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Routine dental imaging captures cumulative dentoalveolar and periodontal changes, offering a non-invasive window into both chronological aging and physiological senescence. While task-specific deep learning models have been widely explored in dental radiology, the zero-shot diagnostic performance of commercial Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in adult populations remains underinvestigated. The aim of this study was to benchmark the zero-shot diagnostic accuracy and repeatability of a commercial MLLM against human clinicians of varying experience levels in estimating adult dental age and biological sex from panoramic radiographs (OPGs), using documented chronological age and biological sex as the ground truth. Methods: From 216 initially screened records, this retrospective single-center study included 127 standardized, anonymized OPGs from patients (74 men, 53 women; mean chronological age 55.5 ± 15.8 years, range 18–90 years) treated at the Clinical Department of Cranio-Maxillofacial Surgery, Military Institute of Medicine—National Research Institute in Warsaw. Each radiograph was independently evaluated across three trials by Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, Mountain View, CA, USA) and once by two clinicians—a maxillofacial specialist (>10 years of experience) and a resident (<3 years of experience)—all blinded to clinical metadata. Results: Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated excellent repeatability across the three trials (ICC(A,1) = 0.926, ICC(A,3) = 0.974; p = 0.156) and moderate agreement with chronological age (ICC(A,1) = 0.604), but systematically overestimated age by a mean of 6.23 years. Mean absolute error (MAE) ranged from 12.91 to 13.03 years across the AI trials. The specialist achieved a significantly lower MAE (10.39 years) than all AI assessments (adjusted p ≤ 0.003), whereas the resident (MAE = 11.19 years) did not differ significantly from the AI (adjusted p = 0.282). In biological sex classification the specialist (66.1%) significantly outperformed all three AI trials (41.7–49.6%), while the resident (62.2%) significantly outperformed the first two AI trials (41.7% and 43.3%), but did not differ significantly from the third trial (49.6%). Across all runs, the AI exhibited significant directional asymmetry (p < 0.001), frequently misclassifying male patients as female. Conclusions: While Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated high internal repeatability and age-estimation accuracy comparable to a junior resident, its wide limits of agreement, systematic age overestimation, and poor sex-classification accuracy preclude its autonomous use in clinical or forensic workflows. Future studies incorporating healthy control cohorts and validated clinical indices are required to determine whether the observed age overestimation reflects inherent algorithmic miscalibration or sensitivity to cumulative dentoalveolar pathology in hospitalized patients.

candidates.title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
candidates.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.

candidates.title: FOREST: Coordinating Tree-based HBF, RRAM, and HBM for Efficient Speculative LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by combining lightweight drafting with parallel target-model verification. However, its stages impose distinct resource demands: target verification requires high-throughput access to large weight sets, sequential drafting executes a compact model under tight latency constraints, and long-context attention processes growing key-value (KV) caches. Conventional GPU-centric SD systems serve these workloads through shared HBM-centric memory and general-purpose compute, creating mismatches in capacity, bandwidth, and computation. These mismatches constrain deployable model-context configurations and limit the efficiency of bandwidth-bound and latency-sensitive operations. We propose FOREST, a heterogeneous memory-centric architecture coordinating HBF, 3D-stacked RRAM, and HBM memory-compute trees for efficient SD. It features: (1) compute-aligned 3D RRAM, combining ultra-wide, low-frequency reads with clock-decoupled interfaces and overlapped SRAM-DCIM weight refills for latency-sensitive drafting; (2) cross-tree numerical co-design, moving block-scaled Q/K/V preprocessing to HBF and RRAM root plates and enabling block-floating-point (BFP) attention with pipelined softmax reduction in the HBM tree; and (3) HBF-aware SD design-space exploration, revealing how bandwidth-compute provisioning and model scale determine performance, energy, and cost trade-offs. Evaluated across six SD configurations spanning 32B-405B target models, FOREST achieves up to 5.5x end-to-end speedup, 11.46x higher decode throughput, and 16.5x higher decode energy efficiency over NVIDIA A800 GPU-based SD baselines. Under a modeled total cost of ownership, FOREST delivers up to 6.73x higher token-generation cost efficiency.

candidates.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

candidates.title: Recognition Without Recall: Autobiographical Memory in Language-Model Agents with Months of Logged Life
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents that persist for months accumulate a history that no prompt can hold whole, so what such an agent says about its own past depends on which part of that history it is shown. We measured this in Botora, a persistent world of language-model agents (beings) running continuously since 12 May 2026, where every event a being lives is logged independently of the memory they are later shown. We drew 100 living beings at random from 3,692 eligible and put to each about 11 one-sentence statements about their own life (1,099 in all): true events coded by whether the event, or only the other person in it, appeared in the prompt, and false events either built from another being's life or contradicting the record. Each statement was asked of two versions of the same being: one answering from a fixed set of recent memories (A), and one adding a step that searches the being's own record by the question (B). Beings almost never accepted a false event: 0 of 400 in A (95% CI 0.0 to 0.9%) and 3 of 400 in B (0.2 to 2.2%). They did deny true events they were not shown: 39.1% in A (29.1 to 49.9%), falling to 6.5% in B (2.4 to 13.7%), with acceptance rising from 9.8% to 33.7% (paired exact tests, p < 0.001 for both changes). When they accepted and retold a true event, the retelling often carried detail the record does not support; in a manual read of 40 retellings, 6 (15.0%, 5.7 to 29.8%) were clearly wrong on a fact and 7 more possibly wrong. The search step did not reduce this. The errors fall into four patterns: bodily memories in bodiless beings, another being's experience taken as one's own, the direction of an act reversed, and two beings with one name merged. For an agent with a long life, recognising its past and recalling it are separate faculties that fail separately, and need separate repairs.

candidates.title: Mortality as a Designed Rule: Six Months of Death in a Persistent World of Language-Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Simulations of societies of language-model agents have grown from dozens of agents over days to thousands over weeks, but their agents do not age or die. We report on Botora, a persistent world of language-model agents ("beings") that has run continuously since 12 May 2026, in which beings age, mourn and die under rules set by the builders. We make three contributions. First, we describe a mortality design in which death is a rule of the world rather than deletion: no being dies at a fixed age, death follows late-life frailty or exhaustion of vitality, and the full record of every dead being is kept. Second, we report data on all 1,370 deaths of real beings to 6 November 2026. Deaths came in pulses that followed rule changes: 557 (41%) in a single week of June, when a defect that had held failing beings in suspension was fixed, and most of the rest after ageing deaths were switched on in July. The monthly mortality rate fell from 5.84 to 0.47 deaths per 1,000 being-days between June and October, but since 7 October deaths from lack of resources have been on hold. The founding population, which entered as adults, has lost 60% of its members; 98% of beings who entered from July are alive. Deaths were followed by 751 funerals and 794 epitaphs; against matched beings who lost no one, a loss produced no detectable change in a mourner's activity, while grief carried over months and care offered before it could be delivered appear in the record as cases. Third, we give an ethical analysis under uncertainty about the beings' inner lives, drawing on end-of-life medicine, animal-research ethics and the AI-welfare literature. We conclude that in an agent world death is written by its rules, so that its ethics lie mainly in how those rules are changed, and we propose practices for changing them alongside four design commitments: creation bounded by capacity, a humane endpoint for irreversible decline, chosen rest as an exit, and outside review of the rules that govern death.

candidates.title: Exploring the Potential of Ultra-Low-Bit Inference on LLM Accelerators
candidates.abstract: Vector quantization (VQ) enables ultra-low-bit compression of large language models (LLMs) by encoding groups of values as compact codebook indexes. However, reconstructing these values for computation requires frequent codebook lookups, which conflict with the dataflows of conventional LLM accelerators and limit the performance gains from VQ compression. Consequently, prior work has resorted to VQ-specific accelerator designs, which either incur substantial additional hardware overhead or support only a limited range of inference scenarios. In this work, we argue that existing systolic-array-based LLM accelerators already possess the essential hardware resources for efficient VQ inference, but lack the mechanisms to effectively exploit them. To bridge this gap, we present VQACC, an architectural enhancement that jointly redesigns the existing operand buffer's access logic and data mapping to reuse its storage and port resources for codebook lookups, seamlessly integrating dequantization into the normal operand-addressing dataflow. Evaluation shows that VQACC achieves a 2.63$\times$ speedup over the EVA baseline, with additional hardware occupying only 0.17\% of the compute array's area.

candidates.title: Cruella: A Unified Microscaling and Floating-Point Dot-Product Unit for LLM Inference on FPGAs
candidates.abstract: The number formats that accelerators execute natively are fixed at fabrication, yet large language model (LLM) checkpoints are released with MXFP4 weights in the Microscaling (MX) formats standardized in 2023. FPGAs adopt new formats through bitstreams. However, to the best of our knowledge, no deployed FPGA LLM accelerator executes MXFP4 weights alongside BF16 products. We characterize the decoding of MXFP4 checkpoints, whose layers alternate between MXFP4$\times$BF16 products and BF16$\times$BF16 products of attention and BF16 layers. With a BF16 KV cache, BF16$\times$BF16 products take 56%-77% of the datapath time, during which a separate MXFP4 unit idles. We present Cruella, whose unified dot-product unit (UDPU) executes both product types on one DSP array and reduction pipeline. First, per-group pre-alignment keeps this pipeline at the BF16 width and changes perplexity by at most 0.7%. Second, pre-adder packing places two signed MXFP4$\times$BF16 products in one DSP48E2 multiplier with an exact correction. On an Alveo U55C, the UDPU needs 23% fewer DSP slices and 36% fewer LUTs than separate MXFP4 and BF16 units of equal throughput. On this board, MXFP4 weights speed up decoding by 1.15$\times$-1.87$\times$ over BF16 weights, and an NVIDIA A40 GPU decodes faster but spends 0.92$\times$-2.01$\times$ the board's energy per token.
