candidates.title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection
candidates.abstract: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.

candidates.title: 9253-GRP Efficient Memory Management for LLM Inference on Constrained Memory Devices
candidates.abstract: Large Language Model inference on memory-constrained devices suffers from delay due to thrashing. Since models with billions of parameters often cross the memory limit, it becomes imperative to keep the weights on disk and fetch them on demand. As a result, the inference procedure faces delay due to the constant swapping in and out of model parameters between disk and memory. In this paper, we establish this problem by comparing the existing methods in the literature. We also propose a solution to this problem, which is an efficient eviction and prefetching scheme.

candidates.title: Traffic Police Gesture Recognition with Large Language Model Agents for Autonomous Vehicles
candidates.abstract: To address the challenges autonomous vehicles face in interpreting traffic police gestures, particularly in complex and non-standard scenarios, this paper proposes a multi-agent framework leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs). candidates.title: Context Engineering & Knowledge Architecture: A Task-Aligned Framework for Designing Information Environments for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) depends not only on their computational capabilities and internalized knowledge but also on the quality, relevance, structure, and accessibility of the information supplied during inference. As LLM-based applications become increasingly complex, prompt engineering alone is insufficient to address challenges involving extensive document collections, persistent knowledge, changing information, multi-stage reasoning, and task-specific information requirements. These challenges create a need for context engineering: the systematic design, organization, selection, and maintenance of the informational environment in which language models operate. This paper develops an integrated conceptual and methodological framework for Context Engineering and Knowledge Architecture. It examines the relationships among contextual representation, long-context management, document structuring, external memory, retrieval augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, information prioritization, and context optimization. The paper proposes the Task-Aligned Context and Knowledge Architecture (TACKA), a reference framework integrating eight functional layers: task specification, knowledge organization, memory management, information retrieval, relevance assessment, context assembly, generation and verification, and continuous optimization. It additionally introduces a task-sensitive context selection model that treats context construction as a constrained optimization problem involving relevance, authority, coverage, recency, provenance, informational redundancy, token consumption, and security requirements. A practical implementation scenario demonstrates how the proposed framework can support research-oriented knowledge systems requiring traceable evidence synthesis across heterogeneous document collections. An evaluation protocol is also presented to distinguish retrieval performance, contextual adequacy, output groundedness, operational efficiency, and security. The central argument is that effective LLM systems require more than access to large quantities of information: they require architecturally organized, task-relevant, verifiable, and dynamically maintained information environments. The proposed framework provides a foundation for designing and evaluating such environments. It is presented as a conceptual and methodological contribution requiring empirical validation rather than as an experimentally established architecture.

candidates.title: ClinDataBench: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in Clinical Trial Analysis Dataset Construction
candidates.abstract: A new drug reaches patients only after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has reviewed its trial evidence, which every application carries as analysis datasets in the Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) Analysis Data Model (ADaM) format that programmers derive by hand from raw trial data, a statistical analysis plan (SAP) and dataset specifications. Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) could take over this work, and a slow-changing industry will adopt them only with evidence of what they get right and wrong. However, work on large language models (LLMs) for CDISC data stops short of evaluating a complete, conformant and reproducible package, and the standard validator checks structure rather than whether each value is derived correctly. We introduce ClinDataBench, built on the public CDISC pilot study: an agent receives 22 Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM) domains, the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and specifications, and must deliver 13 Analysis Data Model (ADaM) datasets, Define-XML metadata and a program that rebuilds them offline. Agents run in containers whose only network route is their model API, restricting online access to published reference outputs during execution. A host-only evaluator scores conformance under the Pinnacle 21 Community (P21) validator, selected derivations, clean reconstruction and effort separately. We compare three settings: Base, which submits the agent’s first package; Self-Refine, which revises it without external validation feedback; and CRITIC, which revises it with the agent’s own validator report. In an exploratory pilot with six models, the three closed models and DeepSeek delivered all 13 datasets in every setting and eleven of their twelve packages rebuilt semantically, while two other open-weight models delivered no complete package. Validator findings ranged from 15 to 64 dataset-rule pairs. Four of six CRITIC workflows had usable validator comparisons, and each reduced its finding count. None reduced its failed derivation count. The package with the fewest findings carried none of the 234 efficacy summary records in the form the specifications define, showing that lower validator finding counts do not necessarily indicate more correct derivations.

candidates.title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
candidates.abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

candidates.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

candidates.title: Large Language Models in Clinical Neurology: A Scoping Review
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for clinical neurology applications, yet their real-world utility, safety, and deployment readiness remain unclear. This review maps the literature on LLMs applied to text-based and text-derived neurology tasks, characterizing current use cases, evaluation strategies, performance metrics, and reported safety concerns. We identify areas with relatively robust evidence, highlight important evidence gaps, and outline key methodological and clinical barriers that must be addressed before responsible clinical adoption. RECENT FINDINGS: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), we searched 4 databases (January 2022 to February 2026) and included 32 studies (2023-2026) spanning 7 neurology subspecialties; 9 were simulation or feasibility studies, 17 analyzed retrospective clinical data, and 6 reported prospective evaluation. Proprietary models predominated; 5 studies used retrieval-augmented generation and 1 used a multiagent framework. Performance was highest for constrained tasks, including binary diagnostic classification (area under the curve 0.75-0.94), information extraction (F1 0.89-0.90), patient-education question answering (accuracy 68%-97%), and ischemic stroke thrombectomy decision support (area under the curve [AUC] 0.92) and lowest for open-ended case-based reasoning (accuracy 42%-54%). Recurrent safety signals included hallucinated and fabricated citations, poor calibration with overconfidence (for example, 100% sensitivity with 27% specificity for epilepsy diagnosis), and a systematic bias toward intervention. On adapted Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies Using Artificial Intelligence (QUADAS-AI) charting, overall risk of bias was low in 1 study (3%), moderate in 16 (50%), and high in 15 (47%), driven chiefly by absent external validation (31/32, 97%). Benchmarked against high-reliability and 6 Sigma standards, reported error rates remain orders of magnitude too high for autonomous use. SUMMARY: Evidence for LLMs in neurology is early, heterogeneous, and limited by scarce external and prospective validation. Current data support only narrow, clinician-supervised uses such as documentation and education, while cautioning against autonomous diagnostic or therapeutic use. Rigorous, prospective, externally validated studies with standardized reporting and explicit safety and ethical evaluation are needed before broader adoption. REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420251082465.

candidates.title: Advanced Context Engineering: A Comprehensive Framework for Intelligent Context Management in Large Language Model Systems
candidates.abstract: The increasing complexity of large language model (LLM) applications has transformed context management from a secondary prompting consideration into a central architectural challenge. Modern AI systems operate across extended conversations, heterogeneous knowledge repositories, distributed computational tools, multimodal information sources, and persistent task environments. Although advances in model architectures have expanded the quantity of information that can be processed within a single inference context, the availability of larger context windows does not independently guarantee effective information utilization, factual consistency, operational continuity, or computational efficiency. This paper introduces Advanced Context Engineering (ACE), a conceptual framework for designing intelligent context management systems that dynamically select, structure, prioritize, retrieve, compress, update, and validate information supplied to large language models. The framework conceptualizes context as a constrained computational resource and proposes an integrated architecture combining hierarchical memory, semantic retrieval, knowledge representation, contextual prioritization, provenance tracking, adaptive compression, and continuous evaluation. The proposed model distinguishes immediate working context from persistent episodic memory, semantic knowledge repositories, procedural instructions, and archival information. It further introduces a context lifecycle encompassing ingestion, classification, retrieval, relevance assessment, composition, utilization, consolidation, and controlled expiration. A formal context optimization model is presented to describe the selection of task-relevant information under token, latency, security, and accuracy constraints. Particular attention is devoted to information fragmentation, long-context degradation, semantic drift, retrieval errors, memory contamination, contradictory evidence, and prompt injection. The paper also proposes a reference architecture, operational algorithms, evaluation indicators, and an illustrative implementation scenario for an intelligent research assistant. These elements provide a foundation for developing AI applications capable of maintaining coherent task representations across prolonged interactions and extensive information environments. The central proposition is that effective context engineering requires more than increasing the amount of information available to a language model. It requires a coordinated system for determining which information should be available, when it should be retrieved, how it should be represented, and under what conditions it should influence model behavior. The expected practical outcome is a modular context management system supporting reliable information selection, contextual continuity, efficient knowledge retrieval, and traceable AI-assisted reasoning.

candidates.title: VidToC: Rethinking Video Token Compression for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.

candidates.title: Research on Anomalous Event Detection and Scene Description for Expressways Based on Multimodal Large Language Model
candidates.abstract: With the continuous expansion of China’s expressway mileage and travel demand, anomalous events are increasingly common. Accurate detection and comprehensive scene description are prerequisites for rational emergency response. Current expressway event detection technologies based on video or radar–vision fusion suffer from high false-alarm and missed-detection rates, reliance on a single data source, and a lack of scene description. This study uses Qwen2-VL as the foundation Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM). An event scenario dataset is constructed from multimodal data of the Jin-Ji (Tianjin-Jizhou) Expressway, and cross-modal spatiotemporal alignment and fusion methods are investigated. The aligned dataset is annotated to create a fine-tuning dataset for event detection. Through supervised fine-tuning, a Domain-Specific MLLM is developed that automatically identifies anomalous events and generates scene descriptions by fusing video and millimeter-wave radar data. Validation using Jin-Ji Expressway reports shows the MLLM significantly reduces false alarms and effectively integrates multimodal data for scene description.

candidates.title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
candidates.abstract: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($Δd' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.

candidates.title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving the basis of individual item-attribute assignments unexamined. This opacity limits the responsible use of AI in measurement. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment. RTA is intended to supplement expert review and empirical validation. In a simulation study with perturbed fraction subtraction items, four LLMs recovered the required attributes and withheld attributes the items did not require. In an empirical study with 11 fraction subtraction items, responses from 536 examinees, four LLMs, up to three temperatures, and 100 replications per condition, CoT-derived Q-matrices overlapped substantially with the reference Q-matrix (mean overlap .809) but less than directly generated Q-matrices (.877), and they varied more across replications. Inspection of the traces linked disagreements to item-type coding, labeling rules, and how operations were expressed as steps. Q-matrices with similar overlap differed in fit to examinee responses. RTA provides inspectable evidence that matrix-level agreement and fit do not.

candidates.title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
candidates.abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

candidates.title: LLMs Memorize Their Own Hallucinations During Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Reasoning domains have shaped the post-training recipes of frontier models even though they are trained and deployed in domains beyond math and code. In this paper, we study the consequences of directly adopting reasoning-centric training recipes, e.g., the use of outcome-based rewards for reinforcement learning (RL), injection of "cognitive" behaviors such as proposing and backtracking from hypotheses in reasoning chains, etc., for knowledge tasks. We hypothesize that these decisions, while useful for reasoning, inadvertently encourage models to memorize hallucinations they themselves generate in their long reasoning chains when trained on knowledge tasks. To study this, we train models with standard post-training, extract their self-generated hallucinations during RL, and track memorization throughout the rest of training. Our experiments on six open models across two model families and two architectures confirm our hypothesis. We find that models' recall of hallucinations reinforced during training increases by 4.83% on average, compared to just 0.17% for self-hallucinations that receive no training signal. In fact, models even memorize false facts that they immediately retract in their reasoning; a backtracking template inherited from reasoning-centric training that has no benefit for knowledge recall. Furthermore, we find that memorization is strongest on the hardest training questions, and rewarding a hallucination makes the model less likely to abstain from it later (by 7.23% on average). Overall, our work identifies and systematically studies a previously unexamined pathway through which models learn hallucinations during training.

candidates.title: Hallucination as Enactment: The Invisible Assumption in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Hallucination in large language models is defined on the output. It is found afterwards, by whoever checks. This paper says the cause comes earlier. Before a model answers, it decides for itself what the input means and what the task is. That decision is an assumption. Nobody sees it when it is made, and every next step builds on it. In Context Psychology this first step is called an enactment. A language model makes it itself, without a fixed outcome. A hallucination is the assumption that later turns out to be wrong. A correct answer rests on the same kind of assumption, which happened to be right. The paper reviews the published research. The parts are known: models infer a hidden task, give all text the same priority, guess rather than say they do not know, commit before they answer, and do not show what they used. The step that connects these parts was not found. Six testable hypotheses follow from the thesis, and the studies found refute none of them. All current measures work on or after the output, or inside the model. None of them fixes the outcome outside the model before the model acts. The paper ends with a practical way of working with a language model, based on the EOCME cycle. Theory: The Holographic Meaning Field, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19385072 EOCME® by Noemeos. candidates.title: Comparing fine tuned embeddings and large language models for detecting multimodal online conspiracy theories
candidates.abstract: TikTok has skyrocketed in popularity over recent years, especially among younger audiences. However, there are public concerns about the potential of this platform to promote and amplify harmful content. This study presents a computational analysis of conspiracy theories on TikTok. By leveraging the official TikTok Research API we collect a longitudinal dataset of 1.5M videos shared by creators in the U.S. over three years. We estimate a lower bound on the prevalence of conspiratorial videos (up to 1000 new videos per month) and evaluate platform changes in association with TikTok’s Creativity Program for monetization, observing an overall increase in video duration regardless of content. In addition, we evaluate the capabilities of recent open-weight Large Language Models, both textual and multimodal, to identify conspiracy theories in short vertical format videos. While these models achieve high precision in detecting harmful content (up to $$98\%$$ ), their overall performance remains comparable to a fine-tuned traditional model such as RoBERTa. Our findings indicate that Large Language Models have the potential to support content moderation strategies on TikTok; however, their deployment involves trade-offs relative to fine-tuned traditional NLP approaches, particularly in terms of performance consistency.

candidates.title: Characterizing Age-Conditioned Affective Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: An age prompt can change how a vision-language model (VLM) rates the emotion evoked by an image. Does the change predict how people of different ages rate that same image? We evaluate 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images using young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts and estimate image-specific age differences from ratings by 822 participants. Without an age cue, models closely track average human valence (median Pearson $r=0.891$). Under an older-adult prompt, 16 of 17 models assign lower valence on average than under a young-adult prompt. Yet after adjusting for image pleasantness, correlations between model and human age effects range from $-0.030$ to $0.093$, against an estimated ceiling of $0.595$. The discrepancy is clearest on 54 sensitive images rated as pleasant. Across models, the older prompt reduces valence by $0.845$ points on average, while older participants rate these images $0.443$ points higher than younger participants. Providing human ratings from other images improves agreement on the direction of age differences, although image-specific fidelity remains modest on 600 held-out images ($r_{\mathrm{part}}=0.105$). These results show why evaluations of demographic personalization in foundation models need human comparisons at the level of individual stimuli. Project page available at https://shahriyar-zaman.github.io/age-conditioned-emotion-reasoning/

candidates.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
candidates.abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a student model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B student models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

candidates.title: Adaptive Self–Human Reasoning: A Universal Framework for Dynamic Switching Between Large Language Model Reasoning and Human Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated increasingly sophisticated reasoning capabilities, enabling them to perform mathematical problem-solving, logical inference, scientific analysis, planning, and complex knowledge integration. Nevertheless, autonomous model reasoning is not uniformly reliable across tasks, contexts, and levels of complexity. Human reasoning, meanwhile, provides contextual understanding, experiential knowledge, critical judgment, and the capacity to interpret situations that may exceed the operational capabilities of computational models. Existing research has investigated chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, tree-based reasoning, self-refinement, human-in-the-loop systems, and human–AI collaborative decision-making. However, these approaches generally emphasize particular reasoning mechanisms, computational strategies, or human–AI interaction arrangements. A general mechanism-independent architecture that treats model reasoning and human reasoning as dynamically selectable, switchable, combinable, and reconfigurable functional configurations throughout the reasoning process remains insufficiently formalized. This paper introduces Adaptive Self–Human Reasoning (ASHR), a reasoning-specific theoretical framework grounded in the Universal Self–Human Model (USHM). ASHR establishes three fundamental operational configurations: Self-Reasoning (S), in which an LLM performs reasoning through its own internal computational mechanisms; Human Reasoning (H), in which a human independently performs or directs the reasoning process; and Self–Human Reasoning (S–H), in which model-based and human reasoning contribute to a shared reasoning task. Unlike approaches that permanently assign reasoning to either an AI system or a human participant, ASHR introduces Adaptive Reasoning Configuration Selection, Adaptive Reasoning Configuration Switching, Adaptive Reasoning Combination, and Adaptive Reasoning Reconfiguration. These mechanisms allow a reasoning process to move between model-directed, human-directed, and jointly organized reasoning according to task complexity, uncertainty, capability, evidence quality, computational resources, human expertise, and risk. A formal architecture is developed to represent reasoning states, configuration selection, transitions, contribution allocation, reasoning continuity, and transition costs. The framework further distinguishes changes in reasoning strategy from changes in the entity responsible for reasoning, establishing an important conceptual separation between internal reasoning adaptation and reasoning-participant switching. Human authority, independent judgment, accountability, cognitive workload, and appropriate boundaries of automation are incorporated into the architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to formally articulate a mechanism-independent, function-specific architecture that integrates autonomous LLM reasoning, independent human reasoning, and combined human–LLM reasoning through adaptive configuration selection, switching, combination, and reconfiguration as a unified reasoning-control principle. This priority claim concerns the specific theoretical integration and architecture proposed here, rather than the broader established fields of automated reasoning, cognitive science, human–AI collaboration, or mixed-initiative systems. The paper establishes a conceptual foundation for intelligent systems that dynamically determine who should reason, how reasoning should be organized, and when reasoning responsibility should transition between artificial and human participants.

candidates.title: A Survey of Query Routing Between Semantic and Knowledge-Graph Retrieval for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems increasingly hold two kinds of external memory: dense vector indexes over text chunks and knowledge graphs (KGs) extracted from the same corpus. Semantic (vector) retrieval is cheap and strong on single-fact lookup; graph retrieval targets multi-hop, relational and corpus-level questions but, depending on design, can consume up to several hundred times more prompt tokens per query plus a costly indexing stage, and it frequently underperforms plain semantic (vector) RAG on simple questions. A growing body of work therefore routes each query to the backend that suits it. This survey is, to our knowledge, the first dedicated to routing between semantic (vector) and graph retrieval. We formalise routing as cost-aware action selection and define oracle headroom and routing regret. We propose a four-axis taxonomy (routing signal, routing time, decision type and learning paradigm) and review routers, structure and source selectors, and the adaptive-retrieval methods they build on. From the full texts of the core papers we extract and compare reported accuracy, latency, token and indexing costs. Our analysis yields eight findings. Three stand out. First, semantic (vector) and graph retrieval are strongly complementary: oracle routing exceeds the best fixed backend by 21.5 points on RAGRouter-Bench and by 55% relative Hit@1 on STaRK-MAG. Second, current routers recover little of that headroom: about 20% on the only dedicated benchmark, and their gains over the best fixed backend are often under one point. Third, whether a query benefits from the graph depends less on hop count than on answer scope, relation type, temporal constraints and the KG's coverage of the query's entities. We close with a reporting protocol and open problems, including corpus-aware and post-retrieval routing, label bias and access control in hybrid stores.

candidates.title: A Study of the Effects of Language on Large Language Model Responses and Human Perception
candidates.abstract: People often feel an idea more strongly in their mother tongue, and they soften a hard message so that the listener is not hurt. This study asks whether chat-based large language models (LLMs) handle hard messages with the same care in English, Hindi and Marathi. Ten industry situations, such as a rejected build, a loan denial and the removal of an engineer from duty, were given to ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini in the three languages. The 90 collected messages were scored with a concept-matched word list that has five harshness categories and four softening categories. The scores were Harshness H, Softening S and Net tone N = H − S, with content coverage and length as extra checks. Differences between models were large (Kendall’s W of 0.30 for N and 0.56 for S). Differences between languages were small and not significant after correction. Gemini wrote short messages with almost no softening (S = 0.06), whereas ChatGPT and Claude used courtesy, regret and offers of help. Gemini also left out more key facts in Marathi (82% coverage) than in English (94%). Each cell holds one response, the word list was built after reading the data, and no human rater was used, so the results are exploratory.

candidates.title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.

candidates.title: Thinking in Streams: Proactive Spatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.

candidates.title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models
candidates.abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.

candidates.title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
candidates.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.

candidates.title: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning for Mammography Vision--Language Models
candidates.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.

candidates.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

candidates.title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
candidates.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.

candidates.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
candidates.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

candidates.title: Label-masking audits of health-record large language model agents pass answers that raise suspicion of drug misuse among recipients who know condition rates: a preregistered synthetic-cohort study
candidates.abstract: Preprint (author's original version); not peer reviewed. Objective: To measure when audits that mask a sensitive label pass large language model (LLM) agent answers from which recipients infer the attribute, by what auditor and recipient know. Materials and Methods: In a synthetic cohort (22,324 persons; drug misuse 15.5%), an LLM agent answered an employer's yearly questions after one of three audits: label masking alone, or with coarsening of literature-named conditions or of the three conditions most correlated with drug misuse. Recipients were given age and sex, the overall rate, or rates by condition. Leakage, the recipient's gain in balanced accuracy when flagging probabilities above 0.5, was measured by an LLM reading the answers (80 persons) and a classifier on the audited record (all persons). Hypotheses were preregistered. Results: Under label masking, the recipient given rates by condition flagged 42% with drug misuse and 10% without (leakage 0.158; 95% CI 0.075–0.240; adjusted p = 0.0042), although its area-under-the-curve gain was not distinguishable from zero. At the generator's correlation strength, merging the three correlated conditions into one name did not reduce classifier leakage by the preregistered 0.005 (reduction 0.0049), leaving 0.151 (0.142–0.162); LLM-measured leakage fell by 0.100 (0.037–0.165; no decision rule). Discussion: Label masking did not prevent inference by recipients given condition rates; merging correlated conditions had different effects in the two measurements. Conclusion: Those designing approval of health-record agents should name the assumed recipient, test audits against the strongest rate knowledge it could hold, and weigh leakage per attribute and measurement against coarsening's cost. candidates.title: LSP-RAG: Latent Scoring Perspectives for Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in open-domain question answering, but often struggle with factual accuracy and multi-hop reasoning due to the incompleteness of the training corpora. A promising solution is Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which supplements LLMs with structured knowledge retrieved from external knowledge graphs (KGs). However, existing KG-RAG methods either rely on large-scale language models (e.g., ChatGPT) to guide the retrieval process, which leads to high computational costs, or suffer from limited retrieval quality when using lightweight language models, particularly under multi-hop scenarios. We propose LSP-RAG (Latent Scoring Perspectives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs), a novel KG-RAG framework that enhances hop-wise KG knowledge retrieval through multi-perspective prompted scoring. Each latent scoring perspective is guided by a combination of two types of soft prompts: a perspective-specific soft prompt induces a distinct prompt-conditioned scoring function over candidate triplets, while a contextual soft prompt evolves with each reasoning hop by encoding the query and previously explored KG triplets, enabling the model to preserve consistency and relevance across multi-hop retrieval. Rather than assuming manually defined semantic roles, these latent perspectives are adaptively aggregated to capture heterogeneous relevance signals during retrieval. This design allows LSP-RAG to perform accurate and robust retrieval using lightweight language models. LSP-RAG achieves superior performance across multiple KG-based Question Answering benchmarks compared to existing retrieval systems, including those that rely on much larger language models, demonstrating its effectiveness under limited computational budgets.

candidates.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: From Foundations to Frontiers
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate strong generative capabilities but remain constrained by static training data, susceptibility to hallucination, and an inability to access current or domain-specific information at inference time. RetrievalAugmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by coupling language models with external retrieval mechanisms that dynamically supply relevant knowledge during generation. In the years since its introduction, RAG has expanded from a single architecture into a broad ecosystem of retrieval modalities, architectural variants, and deployment patterns that is increasingly difficult to navigate. This survey provides a unified treatment of that landscape, organized around five retrieval paradigms: sparse lexical retrieval, structured data retrieval, dense semantic retrieval, graph-enhanced retrieval, and agentic retrieval. For each paradigm, we trace the evolution from foundational concepts to current practice, examining the core techniques, architectural patterns, and design trade-offs that practitioners face. Cutting across these paradigms, we examine two disciplines that shape every RAG system: context management, which governs how retrieved information is selected, compressed, and presented to the generator, and evaluation, which measures retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and end-to-end system performance. To make techniques comparable across paradigms, we ground each in a shared vocabulary for the stages of a RAG pipeline and consolidate representative works along five recurring dimensions: retrieval stage, generation stage, system properties, trust and governance, and adaptability. Our analysis reveals that significant challenges persist. Hallucination is reduced but not eliminated, and retrieval augmentation can mask it from standard detectors. Retrieval quality remains highly sensitive to domain and query complexity. Effective use of long contexts lags behind the rapid growth of context window sizes. Automated evaluation metrics often diverge from real-world user satisfaction. We discuss these open problems alongside promising research directions, including multi-modal and federated architectures, cost-efficient graph systems, and standardized governance frameworks. Together, this survey offers a structured road map for researchers and practitioners navigating this rapidly evolving field.

candidates.title: Understanding the Fundamental Design Decisions of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a critical technique for enhancing large language model (LLM) capabilities. However, practitioners face significant challenges when making RAG deployment decisions. While existing research prioritizes algorithmic innovations, a systematic gap persists in understanding fundamental engineering tradeoffs that determine RAG success. We present the first comprehensive study of three universal RAG deployment decisions: whether to deploy RAG, how much information to retrieve, and how to integrate retrieved knowledge effectively. Through systematic experiments across three LLMs and six datasets spanning question answering and code generation tasks, we reveal critical insights: (1) RAG deployment must be highly selective, with variable recall thresholds and failure modes affecting up to 12.6% of samples even with perfect documents. (2) Optimal retrieval volume exhibits task-dependent behavior—QA tasks show universal patterns (5–10 documents optimal) while code generation requires scenario-specific optimization. (3) Knowledge integration effectiveness depends on task and model characteristics, with code generation benefiting significantly from prompting methods while question answering shows minimal improvement. These findings demonstrate that universal RAG strategies prove inadequate. Effective RAG systems require context-aware design decisions based on task characteristics and model capabilities. Our analysis provides evidence-based guidance for practitioners and establishes foundational insights for principled RAG deployment. Our code, data, and artifacts are publicly available at https://github.com/ShengmingZ/RAG_Benchmark_Code_QA.

candidates.title: Cognitive Biases in Syllogistic Reasoning: A Comparative Study of Humans and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Understanding human cognitive processes for reasoning is a key step towards developing human-level AI reasoning systems. Syllogistic reasoning — a classical form of deductive reasoning — is a well-established paradigm for investigating human reasoning, known to elicit systematic cognitive biases such as belief bias and atmosphere effects. In this study, we compare the reasoning patterns of humans and three state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs), namely GPT-4, GPT-4o and o4-mini, across multiple syllogism types with belief andatmosphere effects. Using an online questionnaire, we examine the biases in human syllogistic reasoning and compare this with the LLMs responses. We identify biases and differences in accuracy between different LLMs and humans. Belief-inconsistent statements, which contradict generally accepted common knowledge, and the atmosphere effect impact human and LLM answers. Our results show that, although LLMs outperform human participants, they exhibit human-like cognitive effects. We further evaluate the new reasoning model o4-mini, which performs nearly perfectly on the syllogism reasoning tasks and compare logic, human reasoning and LLM reasoning.

candidates.title: A Hybrid Retrieval and Reranking Framework for Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the reliability of large language model outputs by grounding generated responses in external evidence. However, the quality of RAG-generated answers depends strongly on the relevance of retrieved evidence, the effectiveness of evidence ranking, and the ability to verify whether generated claims are supported by source documents. This study presents a hybrid retrieval and reranking framework for citation-aware RAG in biomedical and healthcare-related document question answering. The proposed framework uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for document ingestion, parsing, chunking, embedding generation, and evidence retrieval. Source PDF documents are stored in Amazon S3, embedded using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, and indexed using Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. A hybrid retrieval strategy is applied to retrieve candidate evidence chunks, followed by reranking to prioritize the most relevant passages before answer generation. The answer-generation stage uses the highest-ranked evidence chunks to produce controlled, evidence-grounded responses, while a separate judge model evaluates each generated factual claim against the retrieved evidence. The framework was evaluated using 150 biomedical natural language processing and healthcare transformer queries. This evaluation was designed as a pilot-scale proof-of-concept study to examine the feasibility of the proposed hybrid retrieval, reranking, answer-generation, and grounding-evaluation workflow. Across the evaluation set, the system retrieved and reranked 3,000 evidence chunks and generated responses from the top-ranked evidence. Claim-level grounding evaluation identified 1,200 factual claims, of which 1,184 were judged to be supported by the retrieved evidence and 16 were classified as unsupported, resulting in an overall grounding accuracy of 98.7%. The results indicate that hybrid retrieval, reranking, conservative prompting, and claim-level grounding evaluation can support reliable evidence-grounded RAG responses when sufficient source evidence is available. The study also highlights the distinction between internal grounding accuracy and strict citation accuracy, motivating future work on explicit sentence-level citation generation and expanded human expert validation.

candidates.title: Smart Answer Sheet Analysis and Personalized Feedback Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Marking handwritten, descriptive exam answers is still largely manual.An evaluator reads every script, judges whether the student really grasped the concept, and writes a mark.Two evaluators seldom agree exactly, and a single evaluator can drift during a long marking session.This paper presents SAGE (Smart Answer-sheet Grading Engine), a platform that combines optical character recognition, sentence embeddings, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and large-language-model (LLM) scoring in one workflow.An OCR pipeline digitizes scanned or handwritten scripts, the text is converted to dense vectors, and those are matched against an index built from reference and syllabus material.The LLM then scores each answer against the passages retrieved for it, rather than leaning only on what it remembers from training.We want to move past keyword matching and pattern classification, which earlier work finds brittle on descriptive answers, and arrive at scoring that can explain a mark in plain language.We cover the architecture, the scoring pipeline, the module design, the related work behind our choice of a retrieval-based ap-proach, and an evaluation protocol built on OCR accuracy, agreement with human graders and retrieval precision.The evaluation dataset has not been built and no experiments have been run, so the numbers reported here are targets, not measured results.

candidates.title: Structured sparse attention for accelerating long-context diffusion language models
candidates.abstract: Introduction Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs) have emerged as a compelling parallel decoding paradigm. However, the inherent full bidirectional attention at every denoising step incurs quadratic complexity, imposing severe latency bottlenecks in long-context scenarios. Methods We investigate attention dynamics in DLLMs and propose Structured Sparse Attention (SSA), which uses a fast structure-wise algorithm to select and reuse geometric patterns for inference acceleration. SSA combines cached structured patterns with protection of the active decoding region to balance inference efficiency and output quality. Results Our investigation reveals a decrease in average adjacent-step attention changes later in denoising, together with vertical and diagonal geometric patterns that motivate sparse-pattern reuse; the trend varies across inputs, layers, and heads. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SSA delivers significant speedups while maintaining competitive quality against previous state-of-the-art methods on the LongBench and RULER benchmarks. At a 128K context length, SSA achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of approximately 2 × . Discussion These findings support structured-pattern reuse combined with decoding-region protection as an efficient, training-free approach to accelerating long-context DLLM inference.

candidates.title: No Request Left Behind: Tackling Heterogeneity in Long-Context LLM Inference with Medha
candidates.abstract: Deploying million-token Large Language Models (LLMs) is challenging because production workloads are highly heterogeneous, mixing short queries and long documents. This heterogeneity, combined with the quadratic complexity of attention, creates severe convoy effects where long-running requests stall short, interactive ones, degrading system responsiveness. We present Medha, a serving system that eliminates these convoys by introducing fine-grained, preemptive scheduling to LLM inference. Medha makes preemption practical with a co-designed set of mechanisms – including Adaptive Chunking and Stream Pipeline Parallelism – that overcome the perceived inefficiencies and scaling challenges of chunking. Additionally, we present a new parallelism strategy KV-Cache Parallelism to reduce the decode latency and afford interactivity despite very long context. These mechanisms are orchestrated by a Length-Aware Relative Slack (LARS) scheduler, a deadline- and heterogeneity-aware scheduling policy that prevents both the convoy effect and the starvation that plagues simpler policies. Under a heterogeneous workload, Medha improves throughput by 5.7 × while reducing median and 90th-percentile latency by 30 × and 174 ×, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art non-preemptive systems.

candidates.title: Measuring and Charging for Retained Context in Long-Context LLM Services
candidates.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.

candidates.title: VernaSolver: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: The wide use of AI chatbots has changed the way students look for study help, but these tools answer from the large data they were trained on and not from the exact textbook a student must follow. Because of this, their answers may not match the prescribed book, the page numbers they give may be wrong, and support for regional languages is weak. This paper presents VernaSolver, a study assistant that answers a student’s question only from a chosen textbook and shows the exact page number for every answer. The system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): an uploaded PDF is read page by page, split into small parts, turned into embeddings, and stored in a vector database; at question time the most related parts are retrieved, re-ranked by a second model, and passed to a language model that is instructed to answer only from those parts. When the answer is not present in the book, the system says so instead of guessing. VernaSolver also supports single-book and subject- wide search, replies in English, Hindi and Marathi, and generates quizzes and flashcards from the book. The system was built and tested on real course textbooks, and the results show that it produces grounded, citation-backed answers and reduces the effort of preparing study material.

candidates.title: Using Behavioural AI to Fingerprint Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Identifying which large language model (LLM) produced an answer usually relies on semantic prompts, network timing or special tokens. This paper studies a much simpler probe: asking a model for random numbers. We asked ten LLMs of three providers (OpenAI, Google and DeepSeek) to generate a sequence of 50 random numbers between 1 and 10, collected 800 valid answers per model and compared them with a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG). Over all positions, the numbers are almost perfectly uniformly distributed, so a simple frequency test cannot separate the models from a PRNG. The order of the numbers, however, is far from independent. Nine of the ten models avoid immediate repetition and small steps, and in more than 97% of their sequences the first ten numbers are all different, which resembles drawing from an urn without replacement. All ten models most often start with the number 7, and the entropy of the numbers drops at the end of every block of ten positions. These patterns differ between models and can serve as behavioral fingerprints. We trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, a random forest and a logistic regression to recognize the source among eleven classes (ten LLMs and the PRNG). To avoid leakage, identical sequences were removed before splitting, and results were cross-validated and reported with confidence intervals. One sequence of 50 numbers identifies the source with 81.4% accuracy (95% confidence interval 80.5% to 82.2%). Five independent requests of 25 numbers each reach 97.2% (96.3% to 97.9%), and five requests of only 15 numbers still reach 95.5% (94.2% to 96.5%). The most frequently confused sources are the two DeepSeek models (deepseek-v4.1-flash and deepseek-v4-pro) and, separately, gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 and the PRNG. The observations are black-box: they hold for one fixed prompt and a closed set of models and describe behavior, not its cause. The results also caution against using LLMs as sources of randomness.

candidates.title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
candidates.abstract: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.

candidates.title: Quantifying the Intrusiveness of Retrofitting Retrieval-Augmented Generation onto Legacy Software Systems
candidates.abstract: Enterprises increasingly add retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to existing REST and monolithic systems, usually by writing an ad hoc HTTP call into a handler, and have no way to quantify how intrusive that choice is. We present (1) a taxonomy of three retrofit patterns, sidecar, SDK-embed and naive-invasive; (2) the Legacy Intrusion Score (LIS), three code sub-metrics (churn, breadth, coupling), and an extension, LIS-X, with three operational sub-metrics measured on a live system (run-time overhead, fault propagation and silent feature degradation); (3) a static evaluation on five legacy systems, two of them real open-source codebases fetched from their repositories at pinned commits; and (4) a live case study that deploys all three patterns as separate OS processes. The code-level ranking sidecar < SDK-embed < naive-invasive holds in all five systems and under 2,000 random weightings, but it follows from component-wise dominance of the sub-metrics, so it validates the metric rather than testing a hypothesis. In the live study, outcomes are not fixed by definition. The sidecar adds no detectable latency to the legacy endpoint (0.07 ms, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.24]), whereas SDK-embed and naive-invasive add 569 and 475 ms and are not distinguishable from each other (p=0.62). Both pass a 2 s dependency delay on to legacy requests, and when the RAG layer fails fast they keep returning successful responses that no longer contain the AI field. Load on the RAG layer slows the legacy service by 1.51-1.57x on a shared host, and sidecar staleness averages 911 ms with a 2 s polling interval. Retrieval hit@1 is 0.95; three hosted LLMs answer all 12 test questions correctly and a local model 9/12, and the four backends are swapped by changing one request field. All dynamic results come from one host and one system.

candidates.title: Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models and Humans on Curated AI-Generated Intraoral Images
candidates.abstract: Introduction and aims To evaluate the authenticity detection performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using real and AI-generated intraoral photographs and to compare their performance with human evaluators with different levels of dental experience. Methods A dataset of 1,000 intraoral photographs (500 real and 500 AI-generated) across 5 standardised views was constructed from single-institution clinical images and the publicly available AI-Hub dataset. GPT-5.1 (OpenAI), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic), and Gemini 3.0 Pro (Google) evaluated all images through vendor APIs. Human evaluation was conducted using a stratified random subset of 200 images by fourth-year dental students, dentists with ≤5 years, and dentists with ≥6 years of clinical experience (n = 5 per group). Results In the 200-image subset, dentists with ≥6 years showed the highest performance (accuracy: 0.740; F1-score: 0.675), followed by dentists with ≤5 years (accuracy: 0.690; F1-score: 0.557). Across the 1,000-image dataset, GPT-5.1 achieved the highest performance among the MLLMs (accuracy: 0.646; F1-score: 0.452), whereas Claude Opus 4.5 showed the lowest (accuracy: 0.571; F1-score: 0.249). All groups demonstrated substantially higher accuracy for real images than for the curated, visually plausible AI-generated images, with the MLLMs combining near-perfect specificity (0.998-1.000) and low recall (0.142-0.292), whereas human specificity was 0.890-0.990 and recall 0.390-0.540. The mandibular occlusal view showed the lowest accuracy among the MLLM groups. Conclusion Current MLLMs showed lower performance than experienced human evaluator panels, with limited recall for the AI-generated images in this study, suggesting that they are not yet suitable as standalone authenticity detection tools in dentistry. Clinical Relevance The increasing visual realism of generative artificial intelligence-generated intraoral photographs suggests that authenticity cannot be judged from visual inspection alone, and robust validation is needed before such images are used as clinical records, teaching material, or training data for artificial intelligence.
