candidates.title: Large Language Models for Multimodal Fact-Checking: Methodological Advances and Persistent Challenges
candidates.abstract: Fact-checking aims to assign truth values to claims within a specified context. Unimodal fact-checking methods, due to modality fragmentation and inadequate adaptiveness, struggle in complex scenarios where multimodal misinformation is interconnected. The rapid advancement of generative large language models (LLMs) has provided a novel technological paradigm for multimodal fact-checking. With their capabilities in deep semantic understanding and cross-modal alignment, LLMs can significantly enhance the accuracy, interpretability, and generalizability of misinformation detection. Synthesizing representative studies from 2018 to 2026 retrieved via a multi-dimensional keyword search, two-step screening, and citation chaining, we comprehensively survey the subtask arrangements, LLM-based methodologies, and relevant datasets for both unimodal and multimodal fact-checking tasks. Following the standard fact-checking pipeline, we comprehensively review existing methods across four key stages, namely Claim Detection and Extraction, Evidence Retrieval, Verdict Prediction, and Justification Production, providing a structured perspective for method comparison and evaluation. Our synthesis indicates that while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) enhance cross-modal understanding and verification flexibility, fine-grained visual–textual consistency and evidential sufficiency remain critical challenges. We provide a comprehensive survey of fact-checking research and offer insights into the development of next-generation fact-checking systems expected to be more robust, scalable, and adaptable across diverse information environments.

candidates.title: Assessing and Advancing Benchmarks for Evaluating Large Language Models in Software Engineering Tasks
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are gaining increasing popularity in Software Engineering (SE) due to their unprecedented performance across various applications. These models are increasingly being utilized for a range of SE tasks, including requirements engineering and design, code analysis and generation, software maintenance, and quality assurance. As LLMs become more integral to SE, evaluating their effectiveness is crucial for understanding their potential in this field. In recent years, substantial efforts have been made to assess LLM performance in various SE tasks, resulting in the creation of several benchmarks tailored to this purpose. This article offers a thorough review of 291 benchmarks, addressing three main aspects: what benchmarks are available, how benchmarks are constructed, and the future outlook for these benchmarks. We begin by examining SE tasks such as requirements engineering and design, coding assistant, software testing, AIOps, software maintenance, and quality management. We then analyze the benchmarks and their development processes, highlighting the limitations of existing benchmarks. Additionally, we discuss the successes and failures of LLMs in different software tasks and explore future opportunities and challenges for SE-related benchmarks. We aim to provide a comprehensive overview of benchmark research in SE and offer insights to support the creation of more effective evaluation tools.

candidates.title: An Empirical Study on the Code Refactoring Capability of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) aim to generate and understand human-like text by leveraging deep learning and natural language processing techniques. In software development, LLMs can enhance the coding experience through coding automation, reducing development time and improving code quality. Code refactoring is a technique used to enhance the internal quality of the code base without altering its external functionalities. Leveraging LLMs for code refactoring can help developers improve code quality with minimal effort. This article presents an empirical study evaluating the quality of refactored code produced by StarCoder2, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, LLaMA 3, and DeepSeek-v3. Specifically, we (1) evaluate whether the code refactored by the LLMs can improve code quality, (2) understand the differences between the types of refactoring applied by the different LLMs and compare their effectiveness, and (3) evaluate whether the quality of the refactored code generated by the LLM can be improved through one-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting. We analyze the refactoring capabilities of LLMs on 30 open source Java projects. We evaluate StarCoder2, LLaMA 3, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-v3 on their ability to improve static code quality metrics, pass unit tests, and reduce code smells. Our findings reveal that production-grade models such as GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 achieve pass@5 unit test success rates above 90% on multi-file refactorings. LLaMA 3 achieves the highest overall code smell reduction with a median reduction of 15.1%, while DeepSeek-v3 and GPT-4o achieve the greatest improvements in cohesion, coupling, and complexity. StarCoder2 demonstrates strengths in modularity improvements and systematic refactorings. Developers outperform LLMs in complex, context-sensitive refactorings such as attribute encapsulation. We also show that prompt engineering significantly affects LLM performance: chain-of-thought prompting improves StarCoder2’s test pass rate by 1.7% and increases code smell reduction compared to zero-shot prompting. One-shot prompting also expands the variety of refactorings LLMs can perform. These results suggest that LLMs are effective for many refactoring tasks, especially when guided with tailored prompts, but benefit from integration with human expertise for architectural or semantically complex changes. By providing insights into the capabilities and best practices for integrating LLMs into the software development process, our study aims to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of code refactoring in real-world applications.

candidates.title: A Comprehensive Study on Large Language Models for Mutation Testing
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been used to generate mutants both in the research community and in industrial practice. However, there has been no comprehensive empirical study of their performance for this increasingly important LLM-based Software Engineering application. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study evaluating both a wide range of traditional approaches and LLM-based approaches. Particularly, we evaluate BugFarm, LLMorpheus, and our newly designed prompt for mutant generation. The experiments cover both leading open and closed source LLMs, on 851 real bugs from 2 Java real-world bug benchmarks. Our results reveal that, compared to existing traditional approaches, LLMs generate more diverse mutants that are behaviorally closer to real bugs and, most importantly, achieve a 1.8 \(\times\) improvement in real bug detection, defined as the proportion of real bugs whose faulty behaviors can be mimicked by at least one generated mutant. Specifically, LLM-based approaches reach a detection rate of 77.4%, compared to 41.6% for rule-based techniques, representing an absolute gain of 35.8 percentage points. Nevertheless, our results also reveal that these impressive improvements in effectiveness come at a cost: LLM-generated mutants exhibit worse non-compilability, duplication, and equivalent mutant rates than rule-based approaches by 25.9, 7.1, and 2.6 percentage points, respectively. These findings provide actionable insights for both research and practice. They allow practitioners to have greater confidence in deploying LLM-based mutation, while researchers now have a baseline for the state-of-the-art, with which they can research techniques to further improve effectiveness and reduce cost.

candidates.title: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Systems
candidates.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.

candidates.title: LEDGE: An Efficient Simulator for Distributed LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
candidates.abstract: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. An efficient simulator for edge LLM serving must support diverse, fine-grained placement configurations, capture runtime behavior, and accurately predict execution times while keeping simulation overhead low. We present LEDGE, a lightweight simulator for fast, fine-grained evaluation of distributed LLM serving on heterogeneous edge devices without executing tensor operations. LEDGE constructs event graphs supporting non-uniform tensor and pipeline parallelism, estimates execution costs using reusable performance models calibrated from end-to-end measurements, and simulates shared-link contention. We evaluate LEDGE on a heterogeneous testbed of 10 Jetson and Raspberry Pi devices, covering 17 model--precision combinations across 4 LLM families. On Qwen deployments, LEDGE achieves request-level mean absolute percentage errors below 3.6% and a 135.3 times aggregate speedup over physical inference. Performance model calibrated on one LLM family yield 7.44% zero-shot end-to-end latency MAPE across three other families. Further simulations show how shared-link contention affects placement decisions and network topology constrains scaling. Across four edge environments, LEDGE completes 26,773 simulation runs in 83.8 minutes, enabling efficient exploration of deployment strategies under diverse resource conditions and serving objectives. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/gdfwj/LEDGE.

candidates.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
candidates.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.

candidates.title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
candidates.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

candidates.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
candidates.abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

candidates.title: Paradigm Evolution and Engineering Selection of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) suffer from two persistent problems in their parametric knowledge: update lag and factual deviation, which hinder their deployment in professional domains. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects external corpora at inference time, expanding the knowledge boundary without modifying model parameters, and has become the mainstream solution for enterprise knowledge bases, intelligent question answering, and document understanding. This paper divides RAG technology into four stages along its design focus: naive retrieval, precise retrieval, adaptive routing, and agentic reasoning, and examines the principal contradictions and new costs of each stage. On this basis, a hierarchical evolution framework is proposed that cross-compares six levels—retrieval, knowledge, fusion, generation, conflict arbitration, and engineering evaluation—against the four stages, identifying gaps in existing research, especially the unresolved arbitration of multi-source contradictory documents across all stages. The paper also discusses applicable boundaries: when knowledge is already well mastered by the model, when the context window suffices to cover the full corpus, or when the knowledge base is small and sparsely updated, adding a retrieval link only increases latency and noise. Finally, selection guidance is provided along three dimensions: accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, serving as a reference for engineering design and future research.

candidates.title: Large Language Models and Their Architectures for Machine Translation
candidates.abstract: Machine translation (MT) is the automatic conversion of text or speech from one language to another without human intervention. It has evolved from rule-based systems to data-driven methodologies, with neural machine translation (NMT) being a pivotal advancement in translation. Transformer is an encoder–decoder-based deep neural network, which is specifically designed for NMT. Large language models (LLMs) are based on transformer architecture and have deep bidirectional encoding and attention heads, enabling them to learn cross-lingual relationships. LLMs can perform translation through zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is another way to use LLMs for MT systems, relying on knowledge sources like knowledge graphs and unstructured text documents that do not require specific training. Fine-tuning pretrained LLMs on a specific corpus can improve the efficacy of MT systems. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) and QLoRA algorithms can be used for fine-tuning parameters, reducing memory footprint requirements.

candidates.title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

candidates.title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
candidates.abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

candidates.title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.

candidates.title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

candidates.title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.

candidates.title: Scalable Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems for Educational Question Answering
candidates.abstract: AI tutors powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) are increasingly used in education, but their reliability depends on retrieving appropriate instructional content. This study quantifies RAG performance in an educational setting using benchmarks of varying complexity derived from a biotechnology curriculum. We began with a baseline RAG system evaluated on a manually constructed question–answer benchmark, then introduced automated benchmark generation to scale evaluation across RAG configurations and identify the most impactful design choices. We further evaluated the best-performing configuration on textbook-section benchmarks labeled by Bloom's Taxonomy and Webb's Depth of Knowledge. Results show that architectural choices such as retrieval strategy and chunking were associated with larger performance differences than parameter-level adjustments, with Milvus hybrid retrieval achieving higher success rates than Pinecone dense retrieval in this benchmark. Full-textbook retrieval also improved performance on some higher-difficulty questions compared to section-limited search. Together, these findings underscore the importance of systematically evaluating retrieval reliability for AI tutors in complex biotechnology domains.

candidates.title: RoadVerse: A Domain-Specialized Multimodal Large Language Model for Road Distress Detection and Semantic Diagnostics
candidates.abstract: Objectives: Current automated road distress inspection systems are largely confined to visual localization and lack the semantic information needed for informed maintenance decisions. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown substantial potential in general scene understanding, their application to road distress is limited by domain misalignment and a shortage of high-quality, language-aligned datasets. The objective of this research is to develop RoadVerse, a domain-specialized MLLM that bridges visual distress localization with structured textual reasoning for road distress detection and semantic diagnostics. Methods: An automated multi-model collaborative framework synthesizes road distress images and generates paired bounding-box and natural-language annotations, resulting in the SRDD Benchmark. Eight representative open-source MLLMs are evaluated under zero-shot inference and supervised fine-tuning using Synthetic Road Distress Dataset (SRDD) and a manually annotated open-access dataset, with performance assessed in multi-label distress classification, localization and semantic description on four public road-distress datasets. Findings: Experiments on multiple public road-distress datasets show that SRDDbased adaptation consistently improves representative open-source MLLMs across classification, localization, and description tasks. These results demonstrate that structured generative multimodal data can provide effective supervision for domainspecific MLLM adaptation, achieving competitive or superior performance compared with manual-supervised settings. Novelty: This study presents an automated multi-model collaborative framework for constructing the language-aligned SRDD Benchmark. We develop RoadVerse as a unified domain-specialized MLLM for distress classification, localization, and maintenance-oriented semantic description. RoadVerse bridges visual distress localization with structured textual reasoning, extending detection-only pipelines toward integrated road distress detection and semantic diagnostics. Practical Applications: RoadVerse can support automated pavement inspection by converting road images into localized distress information and maintenance-relevant natural-language descriptions. These interpretable outputs can assist transportation practitioners with pavement-condition screening, maintenance prioritization, and followup inspection planning, while the data-generation framework reduces reliance on field collection and expert annotation.

candidates.title: Reasoning Across Relational Schemas with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Relational databases underpin modern information systems, yet real-world data environments are increasingly heterogeneous, distributed, and fragmented across schemas with differing structures, naming conventions, and semantics. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in tasks such as Text-to-SQL generation and schema understanding, their ability to reason across multiple relational schemas remains poorly understood. This thesis investigates cross-schema relational reasoning in LLMs through three connected problems: cross-schema SQL query mapping, analysis of factors affecting mapping success, and schema reconstruction from fragmented databases. First, the thesis presents SQL-Exchange, a framework for transforming SQL queries across heterogeneous schemas while preserving source-query structure. Using schema-aware prompting, template-guided abstraction, and target-grounded value substitution, the framework enables structure-preserving query transfer across semantically different domains. Experiments show that LLMs can generate executable and semantically meaningful mappings, which further improve downstream Text-to-SQL performance, especially in low-resource settings. Second, the thesis analyzes why cross-schema SQL mappings succeed or fail. Using over 100,000 generated mappings, it examines the effects of query complexity, schema feasibility, and mapping flexibility on execution validity, semantic correctness, and structural preservation. Results indicate that complex query structures, schema incompatibilities, and ambiguous mappings significantly reduce performance, exposing key limitations of current LLMs under schema shift. Finally, the thesis studies whether LLMs can reconstruct coherent global schemas from fragmented local schemas in data integration scenarios. It introduces a benchmark for global schema construction based on real-world schemas subjected to controlled transformations, including naming drift, schema fragmentation, and removal of cross-source foreign keys. A deterministic evaluation framework measures executability, attribute recovery, and data reconstruction quality. Results show that even state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs struggle to recover globally consistent relational structures under high ambiguity and limited relational visibility. Overall, this thesis advances the study of schema-level reasoning in LLMs by introducing new methods, analyses, and benchmarks for relational reasoning across heterogeneous databases. The findings reveal both the promise and current limitations of LLMs in understanding, transferring, and reconstructing relational structure.

candidates.title: RSI-Prime: Training Models to Train Models
candidates.abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.

candidates.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
candidates.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

candidates.title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

candidates.title: Compact and Decodable Electrocardiogram Text for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.

candidates.title: Agentic Software Issue Resolution with Large Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Software issue resolution task aims to address real-world issues in software repositories based on natural language descriptions provided by users, representing a key aspect of software maintenance. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs) in reasoning and generative capabilities, LLM-based approaches have made significant progress in automated software issue resolution. However, real-world software issue resolution is inherently complex and requires long-horizon reasoning, iterative exploration, and feedback-driven decision-making that demand agentic capabilities beyond conventional single-step approaches. Recently, LLM-based agentic systems have become a promising research direction for software issue resolution, since the related literature has experienced explosive growth. Advancements in agentic software issue resolution not only greatly enhance software maintenance efficiency and quality but also provide a realistic environment for validating agentic systems’ reasoning, planning, and execution capabilities, bridging AI and software engineering. This work presents a systematic survey of 242 recent studies at the forefront of LLM-based agentic software issue resolution research. It outlines the general workflow of the task and establishes a taxonomy across three dimensions: benchmarks, techniques, and empirical studies. Furthermore, it highlights how reinforcement learning has become an increasingly important training paradigm for agentic systems in software engineering. Finally, it summarizes key challenges and outlines promising directions for future research. The artifacts’ page accompanying this survey is at https://github.com/ZhonghaoJiang/Awesome-Issue-Solving.

candidates.title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
candidates.abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis. Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only. Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings. Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types. Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.

candidates.title: A Review of Video Large Language Models: From Spatiotemporal Representations to Reliable Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Video large language models connect video observations with user needs through natural language, allowing summarization, event localization, question answering, and ongoing interaction to draw on shared model capabilities. Yet accepting more frames or generating longer answers does not establish that a system has retained and correctly used the information required by a task. This review examines video understanding since the emergence of large language models, starting from application needs and proceeding through visual interfaces and representations, information management for long videos, intermediate reasoning, data and training, and capability validation. We first compare the pathways through which visual information enters a language model and examine how temporal computation and learning objectives jointly determine the distinctions a model can make. We then trace observation, compression, storage, and retrieval to explain how efficiency methods make decisions, where they save computation, and under what conditions omitted information can be recovered. On this basis, we distinguish relational organization, active observation, and judgment revision as functions of video reasoning, and analyze the roles of text, spatiotemporal anchors, latent features, and tool operations. The analysis indicates that fine-grained capabilities require training examples and objectives that explicitly distinguish the relevant changes; efficiency on long videos requires attention to both information retention and subsequent access; and the value of additional reasoning should be measured by the specific errors it corrects. We connect these findings to sample organization, parameter updates, process feedback, and diagnostic experiments, and discuss the conditions under which predictive and language learning, persistent memory, and transfer to generation and action can be effective. The resulting analysis supports technical choices under specific task requirements. Project repository: https://github.com/LeslieZhoa/Awesome_Video_Large_Language_Models

candidates.title: A Grammatical Correction Method for English Writing Based on a Multimodal Large Language Model
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence has been booming in the field of natural language processing, but the existing intelligent algorithms for grammatical correction of English writing mostly focus on single text modal information, making it difficult to mine multi-dimensional features, and the accuracy is poor when dealing with complex errors and subtle deviations. Therefore, a method for grammatical correction of English writing based on a multimodal large language model is proposed. The subword granularity segmentation method and NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) segmenter are used to preprocess the text, and a semantic encoder based on BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) and Bi-GRU (Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit) is constructed to obtain semantic information. Gating units are added to each modal feature to achieve fusion. In the decoding stage, a hybrid attention mechanism is used to balance the probability by borrowing the replication mechanism, and beam search is combined with a length factor optimization strategy to complete the correction. Experiments show that the overall average F0.5(F-measure with β=0.5) score reaches 0.512, which is 21.1% higher than the comparison method. In terms of GLEU (General Language Evaluation Understanding (metric)) score, the data scale is 12.7% ahead when it is small, and it is 14.2% ahead when it is increased, and the performance fluctuation is only 1/3 of the comparison method. Experiments show that this method significantly improves the accuracy of error correction and provides a reliable and efficient solution for this field.

candidates.title: SchedOps-Bench and Vardiya: a live benchmark and an open harness for language-model agents in batch job scheduler operations
candidates.abstract: Batch job schedulers run the nightly file transfers, scripts and database loads of many organisations, and their administrators spend much of their time on routine repairs: a rotated password, a broken key permission, a held lock, a full disk, a wrong date pattern in a file name. I present SchedOps-Bench, a live benchmark in which a language-model agent acts as the scheduler administrator in a Docker lab with a real scheduler (JS7), two Linux agent hosts, an SFTP server and a PostgreSQL database. Each scenario really breaks the site, gives the agent a ticket that does not name the root cause, and judges the episode only by the end state read from the servers, with separate verdicts for partial, false green and harmful outcomes. The benchmark has 165 scenarios in six sets, each validated in both directions. I also present Vardiya, an open harness that aims to help small and mid-sized models adapt to this work, and compare three rungs: a bare model (zero by construction), a tool-equipped model with only the access layer, and Usta, the same model inside the full harness. The main measured gain is access: with tools, a light hosted model solves 15 of 15 development episodes. The harness adds step efficiency (8.3 against 14.1 steps on average) and, with a weaker model on the hidden test set, 11 of 27 against 8 of 26 correct with 1 against 4 harmful outcomes, a difference that is not statistically significant. With a small local model (qwen3:14b) on the development set, which the harness was tuned on, the harness removed all harmful outcomes (0 against 10 of 16) and raised correct episodes from 3 to 9. On the hard tier there is no correctness gain: on the 17-scenario hard hidden test set both arms are correct in 0 episodes. I release the lab, scenarios, harness, raw episode evidence and analysis scripts under Apache 2.0, and I present the hard tier as an open challenge.

candidates.title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
candidates.abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

candidates.title: Small language models are agentic but not autonomous in greenhouse climate control
candidates.abstract: Agentic large language models (LLMs) are proposed for cyber-physical control, yet evidence on how reliably small open-weight models turn sensor context into actuator commands is scarce. We present a reproducible benchmark grounded in an operational ESP32-based greenhouse controller: ninety-six generated test cases run against the production tool schema and prompts, scored deterministically, with the controller’s rule-based fallback ported verbatim as baseline. Four quantized models (3–14 B) ran on a pinned llama.cpp stack in two locked environments two months apart (12,000 scored runs). Three findings dominate. Autonomous self-initiation is far less reliable than command execution: models executing 65–100% of chat commands fall to 0.4–64.6% when acting unprompted. Model rankings are environment-conditional: one environment favoured Qwen2.5-7B over the 14B (McNemar p = 0.016; cluster-robust GEE p = 0.084), the other decisively reversed it at identical seeds ( p < 0.001; 77.5% cross-environment agreement), requiring re-benchmarking on the deployment stack. The rule baseline matches the second-best model with the best refusal behaviour: the LLM’s measured value is language-mediated actuation, knowledge capture, and auditability, not superior regulation. Field telemetry and thermal replay show the hybrid controller running unattended through the growing season, rules holding the safety-critical floor. All instruments and both environments’ traces are released.

candidates.title: Mixed-Precision Quantization for Language Models: Techniques and Prospects
candidates.abstract: The rapid scaling of Language Models (LMs) has resulted in unprecedented computational, memory, and energy requirements, making their training and deployment increasingly unsustainable. Quantization has emerged as a crucial compression technique for reducing model size, alleviating memory bottlenecks, and accelerating inference. However, while uniform low-bit quantization (e.g., INT8, INT4) provides significant efficiency gains, it can degrade accuracy in sensitive components of transformer-based LMs. Mixed-precision quantization offers a promising alternative by selectively allocating precision across layers or within tensors to strike a balance between efficiency and accuracy. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of Mixed-Precision quantization frameworks for LMs (MXPLMs). We first review quantization fundamentals, including uniform and non-uniform quantizers, quantization granularity, and methods widely used in post-training quantization. We then categorize and compare recent MXPLM frameworks according to their bit allocation strategies and precision configurations across weights, activations, and key-value caches. A comparative analysis highlights differences in perplexity, zero-shot task performance, and deployment trade-offs. Furthermore, we contrast MXPLMs with earlier mixed-precision quantization methods for deep neural networks, identifying strategies that transfer and those that face challenges in the LM setting. Then, we discuss quantization-compatible hardware, KV cache and mixture-of-experts quantization, and summarize open issues and future directions, including hardware-aware design, activation quantization, and scalable optimization methods for billion-parameter models.

candidates.title: Precision vs. Pragmatics: Benchmarking Post-Training Quantization Trade-offs in Sovereign Korean Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The rapid deployment of Sovereign Large Language Models (LLMs) in South Korea requires balancing high computational efficiency with strict preservation of linguistic pragmatics, particularly hierarchical honorifics (Jondaetmal) and cultural context. While 4-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) significantly reduces memory footprints for edge deployment on Neural Processing Units (NPUs), its impact on culturally sensitive Korean generation remains underexplored. In this study, we empirically benchmark the memory efficiency and pragmatic fidelity of 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization applied to a 2.8-billion-parameter Korean sovereign LLM (EEVE-Korean-Instruct-2.8B-v1.0) on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Our results demonstrate that NF4 quantization reduces model memory footprint by 67.2% (from 5.64 GB in FP16 to 1.85 GB in INT4) while preserving grammatical honorific structure in formal workplace communication.

candidates.title: Cognitive Offloading with Large Language Model Agents in Cybersecurity Education: Perceived Burden and Engagement in a Single-Cohort Study with Ten-Year Institutional Context
candidates.abstract: Practice-oriented cybersecurity education often requires novice learners to build target web systems by hand before security analysis begins, imposing extraneous cognitive load. An earlier study introduced a Red/Blue teaming model in which a large language model (LLM) agent builds the target systems (vibe coding) under Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) control, so that learners audit, attack, and defend. This single-cohort study examines learner-level evidence from the 2026 cohort (n = 34) of a university web-security course, set against institutional Course-Quality-Improvement (CQI) satisfaction records for nine of the ten academic years 2017–2026. Evidence comprised self-reported coding-effort logs (n = 25), single-item final-course survey measures (n = 27), and peer cross-evaluation scores (71 ratings). Logged total coding effort had a median of 3.8 h. In the final-course survey, 96% agreed implementation burden had decreased and 93% that deeper engagement in vulnerability analysis and defense design was possible (raw means 4.67 and 4.44 of 5; Wilcoxon p < 0.001). The 2026 CQI score (91.55) ranked second among the nine records (descriptive). In this single-institution context, delegating system construction to an LLM agent was associated with lower perceived implementation burden, greater reported security-analysis engagement, and high satisfaction; multi-site replication is required.

candidates.title: Proposed new words and collective identity in human and language model agent groups
candidates.abstract: Groups develop distinctive words even when ordinary expressions are sufficient. Such words can symbolize collective identity, and observational studies link language use to community attachment. We examined identity change in temporary groups of one human and four disclosed large language model (LLM) agents, comparing discussions with and without a neologism proposal across recruitment waves. We recruited 100 Japanese participants in two sequential waves; an agent proposed a new word only in the first wave. Mean collective identity change did not differ significantly between waves. Within the proposal wave, favorable ratings of the proposed word were associated with change in identity, but this association did not survive correction for multiple testing (adjusted $$p=0.229$$). The three-way interaction among recruitment wave, message count, and team impression had a nominal $$p=0.027$$ but did not survive correction (adjusted $$p=0.082$$). In a sensitivity analysis, the interaction was not significant after adjustment for midpoint identity (nominal $$p=0.078$$; adjusted $$p=0.624$$). The nonsignificant between-wave comparison and exploratory associations that did not survive correction, together with wave confounding and post-discussion evaluations, limit causal inference and motivate randomized studies with repeated measures to test whether proposed group language affects identification.

candidates.title: Kompass: An Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Personalized German University Admissions
candidates.abstract: The German higher education system offers tuition-free, world-class education, yet Indian students face a labyrinth of bureaucratic complexity—including the APS certificate, Uni-Assist, Blocked Accounts, and Anabin degree recognition—that is poorly served by generic Large Language Models. This paper presents Kompass, a public-facing Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed as an expert advisor for German admissions. Kompass employs a Hybrid Database Architecture (relational SQL + pgvector) to ground its responses in 6,000+ university programs and 100+ verified policy documents. A deterministic ”Pre-Flight Execution” router classifies user queries and invokes specialized Python tools for math, SQL filtering, OCR-based document parsing, and live web search, eliminating LLM hallucinations. Evaluation under adversarial testing demonstrates a 0% hallucination rate on fabricated universities and a 0% UI crash rate under API stress, with end-to-end response latency under 3.5 seconds. This work serves as a proof-of-concept for low-cost, domain-specific Agentic RAG systems across sectors. candidates.title: Sniffing Large Language Models Over the Air
candidates.abstract: 1. Introduction TokenSniffer is an offline research pipeline for analyzing encrypted network traffic associated with large language model (LLM) interactions. It uses observable frame metadata to address three tasks, from detecting LLM usage to identifying the model deployment and recognizing the type of task being performed. LLM Usage Detection uses a LightGBM classifier to distinguish LLM traffic from ordinary application traffic. The training and evaluation scripts support fixed data splits and report test accuracy and macro-F1. Deployment Classifieridentifies the provider–model deployment associated with an LLM interaction. It uses a multiscale gated temporal convolutional network with masked attention pooling to classify sequences based on patterns across frames. Deployment-Specific Task Recognition trains a separate classifier for each model deployment. Each classifier predicts one of eight task categories, including writing, reasoning, mathematics, and coding. The training objective combines cross-entropy with weighted supervised contrastive learning to account for the relationship between augmented views of the same capture and examples from different captures. 2. Key Features Consistent traffic representation. All three stages use prepared sequences with 1,024 frame positions. Frame direction, normalized absolute frame length, and standardized log inter-frame arrival time are represented as separate input channels. Longer sequences are truncated and shorter sequences are padded with zeros. Normalization statistics are estimated from the training split and reused for validation and testing. Traffic sequence augmentation. The task recognition component supports timing jitter, frame dropout, and subsequence sliding. Training uses the original sample and its augmented views. The contrastive objective assigns each positive example from the same capture four times the weight of a positive example from a different capture before normalization. Training and evaluation with fixed splits. The included configurations and README commands support training with seeds 42–46. The neural classifiers select checkpoints using validation macro-F1 and evaluate those checkpoints on the held-out test split. Separate run directories make it possible to retain the outputs for each seed. 3. Package Contents TokenSniffer_source.zip contains the following files and directories under code/. llm_detection/ contains the LightGBM detector, frame preprocessing, data splitting, training, evaluation, and repeated-run scripts. deployment_classifier/ contains the deployment classifier, its training configuration, and entry points for preparing data, training, and prediction. task_recognition/ contains the task recognizer, augmentation methods, weighted contrastive loss, and training configurations for nine deployments. requirements.txt in each component lists the Python dependencies for that component. README.md documents the input format, task labels, expected directory structure, and commands for training and evaluation. 4. Basic Usage Extract the archive and create a Python 3.10 or later environment. Install the dependencies for the component you plan to run using its requirements.txt. Prepare the labeled JSONL records as described in the README. Each record contains aligned arrays for signed frame lengths and inter-frame arrival times. Use a fixed split manifest for LLM usage detection and separate training, validation, and test files for the neural classifiers. Run the training command for the selected component. For deployment classification and task recognition, set PYTHONPATH to that component’s src/ directory before running its training or prediction entry point.

candidates.title: On the Use of Large Language Models for Inter-Model Consistency Specification
candidates.abstract: Cyber-physical systems are developed using heterogeneous modeling frameworks that address different engineering concerns and abstraction levels. In practice, models from mechanical, electrical, and software engineering coexist across development phases, creating the need to specify inter-model consistency despite differences in terminology, structure, and execution semantics. A first step of such a specification is to identify which modeling constructs of two frameworks correspond, that is, whose instances have to be kept consistent, and along which dimensions. In this paper, we investigate how well Large Language Models (LLMs) perform this correspondence identification for pairs of modeling constructs, compared with expert references. We use two gold-standard datasets: 90 automotive construct pairs across AUTOSAR, ROS 2, CAD, Simulink, and a brake specification metamodel, annotated by three experts, and 32 smart-grid construct pairs across three IEC metamodels, whose reference labels are derived from a published rule-based integration. Each pair is labeled on an ordinal scale along three dimensions: syntactic, semantic, and behavioral. Six large language models from OpenAI and Google are evaluated under zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting, together with two agentic systems, OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code, run with web access allowed or disabled. We report Quadratic Weighted Kappa, Mean Absolute Error, accuracy, and macro-F1 with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On average, the LLMs agree with the references beyond chance and beyond string- and embedding-based baselines, but ordinal agreement remains weak to moderate. On the automotive pairs with traceable independent annotations, the agreement of the best configurations with individual experts does not differ significantly from the agreement among the experts, whereas most configurations agree less in the semantic dimension and, on the AUTOSAR–ROS 2 pairs, also in the syntactic dimension. Over both datasets, semantic correspondence is judged more reliably than syntactic correspondence. Vendor differences are small and dimension-specific, and in-context examples improve agreement only in selected dimensions. On the automotive pairs, the ordinal agreement of the agentic systems does not exceed that of the best direct configurations. On the smart-grid pairs, for which their prompts, unlike the direct prompts, define the dimensions in the terms used to derive the reference labels, they reach higher syntactic agreement. Web access does not improve their agreement consistently. Overall, LLMs can support experts in identifying correspondences, but they do not replace expert judgment.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Classification Validation Matching Task
candidates.abstract: Textual data can be grouped and classified with various methods. These include classical topic models such as latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) and newer approaches based on text embeddings, such as BERTopic. We present a method that clusters embeddings in a way similar to the BERTopic workflow, but uses a large language model (LLM) for the final classification. Because classifications by an LLM are not fully reproducible, as repeated runs can assign a statement to different categories, we test whether human raters arrive at the same classification. To validate the LLM classification, we test whether human raters assign statements on 1) drivers of psychosocial risks, 2) solution ideas, and 3) derived interventions to the same categories as the LLM.

candidates.title: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games
candidates.abstract: Agent evaluations report task success and rarely say what an agent did at each decision. We score every decision node of three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned language models (LMs) playing five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight properties from decision and game theory, five of them against a CFR+ equilibrium reference. At each node, the LM also states a belief about the opponent's hidden state in a separate call. Without memory and at temperature 0, stated beliefs sit 0.250 to 0.288 in total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, and where the action responds to the state its agreement with that belief exceeds chance by -0.04 to 0.19. The two calls frame the opponent differently, so the result is a behavioural inconsistency and makes no claim about internal beliefs. Under one prompt and greedy decoding, the LM's action never varies with the state in 10 of the 38 cells where the reference varies its own. Memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders at temperature 0; at temperature 0.2 the cells at 1 fall from 16 to 5 of the 46 informative cells, while the belief results hold. A gate withholds, with a stated reason, any belief score the run cannot support, and seven of the eight non-zero defect rates are attributable to the instrument, a representation, or the LMs.

candidates.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
candidates.abstract: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

candidates.title: A Context-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Personalized Learning and Automated Course Development
candidates.abstract: The rapid growth of digital learning resources has created both opportunity and overload for learners navigating online education. This paper presents EDURAG, an AI-powered personalized learning and course generation platform that combines generative artificial intelligence with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to deliver adaptive, context-aware educational experiences. EDURAG integrates secure user authentication, a personalized analytics dashboard, automated course generation, structured lesson management, progress tracking, and a conversational AI teacher grounded in a curated knowledge base. The platform is built on a modern full-stack architecture using Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS on the client and application layer, with Prisma ORM and SQLite for structured data persistence, and JWT/Jose-based authentication secured by bcrypt password hashing. This paper describes the motivation, system architecture, implementation, and functional modules of EDURAG, and situates the platform within the broader literature on intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, and retrieval-augmented generation. We discuss how the fusion of generative and retrieval-based methods mitigates hallucination and improves factual grounding in AI tutoring responses, while also examining limitations such as data quality dependency, domain coverage, and the ethical considerations inherent in AI-mediated education. The paper concludes that EDURAG demonstrates a practical, extensible architecture for trustworthy, personalized AI-driven learning and outlines directions for future research and development.

candidates.title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

candidates.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
candidates.abstract: This is an earlier single-author preprint. A later revision with additional authors has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Reliability for consideration. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Supplementary aggregate results are available separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24369921. When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

candidates.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
candidates.abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

candidates.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
candidates.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
